title: Object Tracking Using Particle Filter
text:
In this post, we are going to talk about object tracking in videos. In the tracking task, we want to predict the location of an object in the next frame. In the case of particle filter, as well as many other classical tracking algorithms, we make the prediction based on estimated dynamics (which will be explained later) and then update the prediction using some measurements.
Consider the example of the following video of one of the Simpsons couch gags.
We would like to track the position of the gardener at each frame.
Let’s start by explaining the general mathematical idea behind the algorithm. At each time step (or frame in the case of a video), we have some belief (also called prior knowledge) about the position of the object. This belief is based on the information we have from the previous steps. To improve our estimation of the position of the object, we add additional information to our initial belief (or prediction) by measuring the state at the current time step. Using the measurement, we can update, or correct, the state of the object (which is its position). This new corrected estimation is also called posterior.
More formally, we can say our object has some hidden state (position in our case) which will be marked as \(X\). We don’t know this state for sure (that’s why it’s hidden), and we can make an estimation of it. We can also make some measurement \(Y\) of the state, but the measurement is always noisy, which means it is not perfect and gives us some distribution of where the object is, rather than a precise location (if the measurement were perfect, we wouldn’t need any estimation—we would know exactly where the object is).
At each time step the state of the object changes, and we want to use the information from the past and the current measurement to estimate the current state by finding the most probable state. Mathematically, we first want to make a prediction based on the past to form our belief of the current state (which is a probability distribution)
\[
P(X_t \vert{} X_0, \dots, X_{t-1}, Y_0, \dots, Y_{t-1})
\]
Then, we want to make a correction to the prediction by using the measurement from the current time step.
\[
P(X_t \vert{} X_0, \dots, X_{t-1}, Y_0, \dots, Y_{t-1}, Y_t)
\]
In practice, we are going to simplify this by assuming the process is Markovian, which means it only depends on the previous time step. So, the belief about the current state only depends on the previous step’s state.
\[
P(X_t \vert{} X_{t-1})
\]
and the correction adds knowledge of the current measurement.
\[
P(X_t \vert{} X_{t-1}, Y_t)
\]
We can express the last equation using Bayes’ rule as follows.
\[
P(X_t \vert{} X_{t-1}, Y_t) = \frac{P(Y_t \vert{} X_{t-1}, X_t)P(X_t \vert{} X_{t-1})}{P(Y_t \vert{} X_{t-1})}
\]
From this equation, we can see that the current state depends on the probability of getting the current measurement \(Y_t\) given we are in the state \(X_t\) (the likelihood of seeing the measurement if we are indeed in state \(X_t\)) multiplied by the probability of being at state \(X_t\) given we were in the state \(X_{t-1}\) (which is our belief or prior). This is normalized by the probability of getting the measurement \(Y_t\) given we were in state \(X_{t-1}\).

title: Object Tracking Using Particle Filter
text:
Linear Dynamics Model
For making our initial prediction (or belief) we use a dynamics model. This model assumes some relation between the state at step \(t-1\) and step \(t\). We are going to use a linear dynamics model, which means the relation between the steps is linear. As we want to predict the position of a moving object, we can, for example, construct its state as a vector of position \(p_x\) and \(p_y\), and velocity \(v_x\) and \(v_y\), so \(x_t=[p_{x,t}, p_{y,t}, v_{x,t}, v_{y,t}]\). One model that can relate the state \(x_{t-1}\) and \(x_t\) is
\[
\begin{aligned} p_{x,t} &= p_{x,t-1} + v_{x,t-1}\Delta t \\ p_{y,t} &= p_{y,t-1} + v_{y,t-1}\Delta t \\ v_{x,t} &= v_{x,t-1} \\ v_{y,t} &= v_{y,t-1} \end{aligned}
\]
where in our case \(\Delta t=1\). We can also write it in a matrix form:
\[
x_t = Mx_{t-1} + \epsilon
\]
where
\[
M = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\]
The first two rows represent the equation for the new position and the last two rows mean the velocity in both the x and y directions is conserved. We also add some noise because of the uncertainty we have.

title: Object Tracking Using Particle Filter
text:
Visualization of the Process
The process we described so far to go from the state at \(t-1\) to the state at time \(t\) can be visualized in the following figure which describes a 1D case.



In the top left plot, we see the distribution of the position \(x\) (since we are in 1D, the state contains only the position along the x-axis) at step \(t-1\). After applying our dynamics, the distribution moves to a new position without changing its shape. This step is deterministic since we know our dynamics. Because we are not sure about the dynamics, we add noise, or uncertainty, to the distribution which makes it wider, as in the bottom right figure. Finally, we add additional information by making a measurement, which corrects the position and decreases the uncertainty.

title: Object Tracking Using Particle Filter
text:
Particle Filter
We can look at a distribution as a representation of particles with different weights. Big particles are located where the probability is high and small ones where it is low.



The process is similar to the one described before. We start with \(N\) particles with different weights that describe the distribution of the state at step \(t-1\). From those particles, we sample a new collection of \(N\) particles where a bigger particle has a higher probability of being chosen, and we can sample the same particle more than once. For the new collection of particles, we apply the dynamics and make the deterministic drift. Then, we add some noise to the particles to extend the distribution. Finally, by using measurements, we assign weights to the particles according to the likelihood of getting this measurement if the state is really as represented by the particle.



As usual, it will be clearer if we code an example, so let’s code it.

title: Object Tracking Using Particle Filter
text:
Let’s code it
In this section, we are going to implement a particle filter in Python to track the gardener in the video from the beginning.
The full code can be seen here.
First, we need to import the packages we will use
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import cv2  # openCV
Next, we initialize a video capture object to read the frames from the video and read the first frame.
# create video reader object and read the first frame
cap = cv2.VideoCapture('simpson.avi')
ret, image = cap.read()
We start the particle filter by choosing the number of particles we will use (the more particles, the more accurate the distribution will be, though at a higher computational cost), and set an initial state. We choose the state to be [x coordinate of the center of the gardener’s bounding box, its y coordinate, the velocity in the x direction of the bounding box, the velocity in the y direction]. We are also going to assume the size of the bounding box is constant (though generally speaking, it can be part of the state).
num_of_particles = 250
s_init = np.array([81, 169, 0, 0])  # initial state [x_center, y_center, x_velocity, y_velocity]

# bounding box's (half) height and width.
# We assume those are constant
half_height = 118
half_width = 33
The initial state and the size of the bounding box are picked manually.
Before the actual calculation, we create a video writer object to save the resulting video with the tracking.
# get parameters of the video
frame_width = int(cap.get(3))
frame_height = int(cap.get(4))
fps = 20 #cap.get(5)  # frames per second

# create a video writer object
size = (frame_width, frame_height)
result = cv2.VideoWriter('simpson_tracked.avi',
                         cv2.VideoWriter_fourcc(*'MJPG'),
                         fps, size)
For the measurement, we will compare the (normalized) color histogram in the region of interest (ROI) between the original bounding box from the initial state and the new candidate bounding boxes in later frames. For that, we define a function to compute the normalized histogram.
def compute_norm_hist(image, state):
    """
    Compute histogram based on the RGB values of the image in the ROI defined by the state
    Args:
        image (np.ndarray): matrix representing image with the object to track in it
        state (np.ndarray): vector of the state of the tracked object

    Returns:
        vector of the normalized histogram of the colors in the ROI of the image based on the state
    """
    # get the top-left and bottom-right corner of the object bounding box
    # if the bounding box is outside the frame, we clamp it
    x_min = max(np.round(state[0] - half_width).astype(int), 0)
    x_max = min(np.round(state[0] + half_width).astype(int), image.shape[1])
    y_min = max(np.round(state[1] - half_height).astype(int), 0)
    y_max = min(np.round(state[1] + half_height).astype(int), image.shape[0])

    roi = image[y_min:y_max+1, x_min:x_max+1]
    roi_reduced = roi // 16  # change range of pixel values from 0-255 to 0-15
    # build vector to represent the combinations of RGB as single value
    roi_indexing = (roi_reduced[..., 0] + roi_reduced[..., 1] * 16 + roi_reduced[..., 2] * 16 ** 2).flatten()
    hist, _ = np.histogram(roi_indexing, bins=4096, range=(0,4096))
    norm_hist = hist / np.sum(hist)  # normalize the histogram
    return norm_hist
First, we get the coordinates of the top-left and bottom-right corners of the bounding box according to the state. Next, we extract only the ROI from the image. To make the calculation easier, we reduce the range of color values from 256 values to 16 values. The // operator is called floor division. It divides the two numbers and rounds the result down to the nearest whole number. For example, \(245 // 16 = 15\), and also \(255 // 16 = 15\). For each combination of RGB (in the range 0–15) we want to assign a unique number, so we build a base-16 number. Think of a regular decimal number like 163. This number is in base 10, which means we can write it as \(163 = 3 \times 10^0 + 6 \times 10^1 + 1 \times 10^2\). The same principle is used here where the first color channel represents \(16^0\), the second is \(16^1\), and the last is \(16^2\). The range of the new numbers is 0–4095, meaning 4096 unique numbers. We construct a histogram from all the values in the ROI and normalize it by the sum of the histogram so the comparison will be consistent.
Using the previous function, we can create the normalized histogram of the initial state.
# get the normalized histogram of the initial state
# This histogram is the histogram we compare to later
q = compute_norm_hist(image, s_init)
Since we currently have only one state, we duplicate it by the number of particles and set the same weight for all of them.
# for the first frame all the particles are the same as the initial state
# and have the same weight since we don't have uncertainty in the state
s_new = np.tile(s_init, (num_of_particles, 1)).T
weights = np.ones(num_of_particles)
Inside a while loop, we will perform all the steps of the algorithm: sample, predict (and add noise), measure, and reweight.
# go over the frames in the video
while True:
    # sample new particles according to the weights
    s_sampled = sample_particle(s_new, weights)
    # predict new particles (states) according to the previous states
    s_new = predict_particles(s_sampled)
    # go over the new predicted states, and compute the histogram for the state and
    # the weight with the original histogram
    for jj, s in enumerate(s_new.T):
        p = compute_norm_hist(image, s)
        weights[jj] = compute_weight(p, q)
Let’s go over the steps. First, we sample based on the particles and their distributions.
def sample_particle(particles_states, weights):
    """
    Sample the particles (states) according to their weights.
    First, random numbers from uniform distribution U~[0,1] are generated.
    The random numbers are subtracted from the cumulative sum of the weights,
    and the sampling is made by selecting the state whose cumulative weight
    sum is the minimal one greater than the random number. If c[i] is the
    cumulative sum of the weights for the i-th state and r is a random number, the
    state which will be sampled is the j-th state such that c[j] >= r and c[j] is
    the smallest one that holds this inequality.
    Args:
        particles_states (np.ndarray): matrix whose columns are the states
        weights (np.ndarray): weights of each state

    Returns:
        (np.ndarray): matrix of sampled states according to their weights
    """
    normalized_weights = weights / np.sum(weights)
    sampling_weights = np.cumsum(normalized_weights)
    rand_numbers = np.random.random(sampling_weights.size)  # get random numbers from U~[0,1]
    cross_diff = sampling_weights[None, :] - rand_numbers[:, None]  # subtract from each weight any of the random numbers
    cross_diff[cross_diff < 0] = np.inf  # remove negative results
    sampling = np.argmin(cross_diff, axis=1)
    sampled_particles = particles_states[:, sampling]  # sample the particles
    return sampled_particles
The main idea behind the algorithm is as follows: we normalize the weights of the particles and calculate their cumulative sum. We pick a random number between 0 and 1, and subtract this number from the cumulative weight vector we calculated previously. We search for the element with the minimum value that is also above 0. In other words, we pick the first element whose cumulative sum weight is greater than the random number. States with high weights are more likely to be selected (we can select a state more than once).
The next step is making a prediction using the sample we just created.
def predict_particles(particles_states):
    """
    Predict new particles (states) based on the previous states
    Args:
        particles_states (np.ndarray): matrix of states. The rows are the properties of the state and the columns are the particles

    Returns:
        (np.ndarray): new predicted particles
    """
    # the dynamics we use assume that:
    # x_new = x + v_x (x - center position)
    # y_new = y + v_y (y - center position)
    # v_x_new = v_x (velocity at x)
    # v_y_new = v_y (velocity at y)
    dynamics = np.array(
        [[1 ,0, 1, 0],
         [0, 1, 0, 1],
         [0, 0, 1, 0],
         [0, 0, 0, 1]]
    )
    # multiplying the state by the dynamics and add some noise
    predicted_states = dynamics @ particles_states + np.random.normal(loc=0, scale=1, size=particles_states.shape)
    return predicted_states
We use dynamics like the ones we described earlier to predict the new states. For each new state, we also add Gaussian noise to create the predicted states.
For the new particles, we want to measure their similarity to the original ROI. For the measurement, we are going to use the Bhattacharyya coefficient, which measures the similarity between two normalized histograms.
def compute_weight(p, q):
    """
    Compute the weight based on Bhattacharyya coefficient between 2 normalized histograms
    Args:
        p (np.ndarray): normalized histogram
        q (np.ndarray): normalized histogram

    Returns:
        (float): weight based on Bhattacharyya coefficient between p and q
    """
    # make sure the histogram is normalized
    if not np.isclose(np.sum(p), 1):
        raise ValueError('p histogram is not normalized')
    if not np.isclose(np.sum(q), 1):
        raise ValueError('q histogram is not normalized')
    bc = np.sum(np.sqrt(p * q))  # Bhattacharyya coefficient
    return np.exp(20 * bc)  
For each of the particles, we measure the similarity between its histogram and the original one to assign a weight.
Finally, we draw the bounding box on the frame and save it to the video.
    # draw bounding box over the tracked object
    image_with_boxes = draw_bounding_box(image, s_new, weights, with_max=True)
    result.write(image_with_boxes)
To draw the bounding box, we calculate the weighted average over the new states to get the mean state and draw it. We also add the bounding box of the most probable state (the one with the highest weight).
def draw_bounding_box(image, states, weights, with_max=True):
    """
    Draw rectangle according to the weighted average state and (optionally) a rectangle of the state with
    the maximum score.
    Args:
        image (np.ndarray): the image to draw rectangle on
        states (np.ndarray): the sampling states
        weights (np.ndarray): the weight of each state
        with_max (bool): True to draw a rectangle according to the state with the highest weight

    Returns:
        (np.ndarray): image with rectangle drawn on for the tracked object
    """
    mean_box = np.average(states, axis=1, weights=weights)
    x_c_mean, y_c_mean = np.round(mean_box[:2]).astype(int)
    image_with_boxes = image.copy()
    cv2.rectangle(image_with_boxes, (x_c_mean - half_width, y_c_mean - half_height),
                                     (x_c_mean + half_width, y_c_mean + half_height), (0, 255, 0), 1)
    if with_max:
        max_box = states[:, np.argmax(weights)]
        x_c_max, y_c_max = np.round(max_box[:2]).astype(int)
        cv2.rectangle(image_with_boxes, (x_c_max - half_width, y_c_max - half_height),
                                         (x_c_max + half_width, y_c_max + half_height), (0, 0, 255), 1)
    return image_with_boxes
At the end of the iteration, we read the next frame of the video. If there are no frames left, we finish the loop.
    # read next frame
    ret, image = cap.read()
    if not ret:  # if there is no next frame to read, stop
        break
This process continues in the loop, where we use the new states and weights to restart the algorithm and find the bounding box for the next frame.
After going over all the frames, we close the video objects.
# release video objects
cap.release()
result.release()
Time to see the final video with the bounding boxes. The green one is for the weighted average state and the red is for the most probable state.

Note that there is a stochastic element in the algorithm, so the tracking may not work every time. It can be improved by adjusting the number of particles and the added noise.

title: Object Tracking Using Particle Filter
text:
Conclusion
In this post, we went over the particle filter algorithm for tracking objects in a video. We saw just one implementation, but there are other techniques to use it (for example, other measurement methods). Moreover, the algorithm can be applied to more fields than just tracking, since it helps build a general distribution.

title: How to Use Connected Components to Find Sunspots
text:
Sunspots are phenomena on the sun’s surface that appear as temporary dark spots. In the region of the spots, the temperature is lower than the surface around, which makes the spot region look darker.
Although the spots can look small, they are actually huge and can be bigger than Earth.
In this article, we are going to use photos of the sun from SpaceWeather, search for sunspots and determine their size.

title: How to Use Connected Components to Find Sunspots
text:
Getting the Data
The first step is to get an image of the sun from SpaceWeather. We can manually download an image from the website as in the figure below:



Go to the sun photo on the left side and click “no label”


But it will be much nicer if Python gets the photos for us. The simplest way (although it may not work for old photos) is to look at the URL of the photo.
For instance, let’s look at the URL of a photo from the 20th of July 2023: spaceweather.com/images2023/20jul23/hmi4096_blank.jpg. We can see a pattern in the URL we can handle simply.
from datetime import datetime

date = datetime(2022, 7, 17)
url = f'https://spaceweather.com/images{date.year}/{date.strftime("%d%b%y").lower()}/hmi4096_blank.jpg'
In the above code block, we import the datetime class to handle dates. We create a datetime object with the date we want a photo of (in this case, the 17th of July 2022) and then compose the URL for the image using the date.
Now that we have the URL for the date we want, we can read the image data
from urllib.request import urlopen
import numpy as np
import cv2  # OpenCV

resp = urlopen(url)
image = np.asarray(bytearray(resp.read()), dtype="uint8")
image = cv2.imdecode(image, cv2.IMREAD_COLOR)
image = cv2.cvtColor(image, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
We use the urlopen function to connect to the image on the web, and then read the data of the image as a byte array and convert it to a numpy array. We decode that array into an image using imdecode from OpenCV and finally convert it into a grayscale image.



A grayscale image of the sun with sunspots


We succeeded in getting the image of the sun and loading it into our environment. Now we want to find the sunspots.

title: How to Use Connected Components to Find Sunspots
text:
Finding Spots
To find the spots, we use two main techniques. The first one is adaptive thresholding, and the second is connected components.
In regular thresholding, we pick a threshold value (in an uint8 image, an integer between 0 and 255), and if the value of a pixel is above it, we set its new value to 255, otherwise to 0. A more sophisticated method is to use an adaptive threshold—a different threshold for each pixel that depends on the neighborhood of that pixel. For example, the threshold can be the mean of some window or a weighted sum using a Gaussian window. We can also move this value with a scalar to pick a value bigger or smaller than the mean. Again, if the value of the pixel is greater than the threshold, we set it to 255, otherwise to 0. In our case, it can be more convenient to set the sunspots to white (255) and keep the background black. For that, we can use inverse thresholding, which sets to 255 pixels with values smaller than the threshold. The reason to use such thresholding is that the sunspot should be darker than its neighbor regions.
The connected components is a technique to group pixels into blobs in a black and white image. The basic idea behind this algorithm is simple and can be described as follows: start from the top left pixel (we assume it is black) and mark it as belonging to component 0 (all black pixels are considered as background, and we set them to group 0). Continue to the next pixel on the right until finding a white pixel, and set it to 1. If the next pixel is also white, we set it to 1 since it touches another white pixel with the label 1. Continue so up to the end of the row, and then go to the next row. For any white pixel that touches another white pixel with a label, we set it to the same component as the pixel it touches. If the new white pixel does not touch any other white pixel which has already been set to some group, we set it to a new group.



First scan result. We can see pixels with different labels in the same blob. Image from  Wikipedia 


After the first run, we may see pixels in the same blob but with different labels, as in the figure above. To solve it, we search for a relation between the different labels. If we find a white pixel that has a white pixel neighbor but with a different label, we mark those labels as equivalent. For example, in the figure above, labels 1 and 2 are equivalent, and so are labels 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7. We replace the equivalent labels with one label and get the components.



After removing redundant labels. Image from  Wikipedia 


In the figure above, we see that we found two blobs.
You can watch the following video to understand better the process:

Let’s code now!
def find_spots_adaptive(image):
    image_blur = cv2.GaussianBlur(image, (13, 13), 0)
    binary_img = cv2.adaptiveThreshold(image_blur, 255, cv2.ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C, cv2.THRESH_BINARY_INV, 301, 30)
    binary_img = cv2.dilate(binary_img, None, iterations=1)
    binary_img = cv2.erode(binary_img, None, iterations=1)
We create a function to find the sunspots using adaptive thresholding and connected components. We start by blurring the image a little to remove noise and then binarize it using inverse adaptive thresholding with a Gaussian window so that the darker spots will be white and the other pixels will be black. We apply dilation followed by erosion to close small holes which may be present.
    _, _, boxes, centroid = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(binary_img)
On the binary image, we use the function connectedComponentsWithStats. This function returns all the connected components in the image. As already explained, connected component is a blob built from white pixels that touch each other.



Image with three connected components (black background, red, and white). Each pixel in a component touches another pixel in the component. Image from  Wikipedia 


Pay attention that the background itself is considered a connected component. In the boxes variable, we have the top left (x, y) and the width and height of the bounding rectangle of the components (where the first one is the background), and also the total area (in pixels) for each component. The centroid variable stores the (x, y) coordinate of the center of the component.
    boxes = boxes[1:]
    filtered_boxes = []
    filtered_centroid = []
    for (x, y, w, h, pixels), cent in zip(boxes, centroid):
        if pixels < 10000 and h > 10 and w > 10:
            filtered_boxes.append((x, y, w, h))
            filtered_centroid.append(cent)
We continue our function by throwing the first component since it is the background. Then, we want to filter the components and keep only blobs that can be a sunspot. We go over the components and keep blobs with a size greater than 10 pixels and an area of less than 10,000 pixels.
    pixel_size_km = 363.313
    im_rgb = cv2.cvtColor(image, cv2.COLOR_GRAY2RGB)
    oversize = 2
    for x, y, w, h in filtered_boxes:
        cv2.rectangle(im_rgb, (x - oversize, y - oversize), (x + w + oversize, y + h + oversize), (255, 0, 0), 1)
    for (x, y, w, h), (x_cent, y_cent) in zip(filtered_boxes, filtered_centroid):
        r = max(w / 2, h / 2)
        cv2.putText(im_rgb, f'{int(pixel_size_km * r)}km', (x, y - 3), cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 0.4, (0, 255, 0), 1,
                    cv2.LINE_AA)
    cv2.putText(im_rgb, f'{len(filtered_boxes)}', (100, 400), cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 12, (255, 0, 0), 10, cv2.LINE_AA)
    return im_rgb
Finally, we want to mark the spots in the image and estimate the size. To determine the size of the spots, we can find the diameter of the sun in pixels (manually measure it from the image), while we know that the real diameter of the sun is about 1.4 million kilometers. From that, we can convert pixels to kilometers.
We convert our image back to a color image and then draw a red rectangle over the detected spots, and also add text with the radius of the spot, estimated as the maximum between half the width and half the height of the bounding rectangle. At the corner of the image, we also add the number of spots detected.



The final result with the sunspots marked.





A zoom-in to the spots.

title: How to Use Connected Components to Find Sunspots
text:
Conclusion
In this article, we saw how we could get an image of the sun and detect sunspots with their size using Python and OpenCV and techniques such as adaptive thresholding and connected components.
The full code:
from datetime import datetime
from urllib.request import urlopen
import numpy as np
import cv2  # OpenCV

def find_spots_adaptive(image):
    image_blur = cv2.GaussianBlur(image, (13, 13), 0)
    binary_img = cv2.adaptiveThreshold(image_blur, 255, cv2.ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C,
                                       cv2.THRESH_BINARY_INV, 301, 30)
    binary_img = cv2.dilate(binary_img, None, iterations=1)
    binary_img = cv2.erode(binary_img, None, iterations=1)
    
    _, _, boxes, centroid = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(binary_img)
    
    boxes = boxes[1:]
    filtered_boxes = []
    filtered_centroid = []
    for (x, y, w, h, pixels), cent in zip(boxes, centroid):
        if pixels < 10000 and h > 10 and w > 10:
            filtered_boxes.append((x, y, w, h))
            filtered_centroid.append(cent)
    
    pixel_size_km = 363.313
    im_rgb = cv2.cvtColor(image, cv2.COLOR_GRAY2RGB)
    oversize = 2
    for x, y, w, h in filtered_boxes:
        cv2.rectangle(im_rgb, (x - oversize, y - oversize), (x + w + oversize, y + h + oversize), (255, 0, 0), 1)
    
    for (x, y, w, h), (x_cent, y_cent) in zip(filtered_boxes, filtered_centroid):
        r = max(w / 2, h / 2)
        cv2.putText(im_rgb, f'{int(pixel_size_km * r)}km', (x, y - 3), cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 0.4, (0, 255, 0), 1,
                    cv2.LINE_AA)
    cv2.putText(im_rgb, f'{len(filtered_boxes)}', (100, 400), cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 12, (255, 0, 0), 10, cv2.LINE_AA)
    return im_rgb

date = datetime(2022, 7, 17)
url = f'https://spaceweather.com/images{date.year}/{date.strftime("%d%b%y").lower()}/hmi4096_blank.jpg'
resp = urlopen(url)
image = np.asarray(bytearray(resp.read()), dtype="uint8")
image = cv2.imdecode(image, cv2.IMREAD_COLOR)
image = cv2.cvtColor(image, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

spots_im = find_spots_adaptive(image)

title: pathlib — a Better Way to Work with Paths in Python
text:
Photo by  Hermann  on Pixabay
Traditionally programmers in Python handle file and directory paths as strings, either writing the string directly or using modules like os. That can be ugly and sometimes can lead to bugs.
A better way to handle paths is by using pathlib module which is part of the Python standard library, so if you have Python installed, you are good to go.
With pathlib, instead of using strings, we use Path object:
The Path class also has some useful methods that help you start with your path like Path.home() that returns Path object with the path to the home directory of the user, and Path.cwd() that returns the path to the current working directory.
If you look closely at the previous example, you see that we didn’t get a Path object, but PosixPath. The Path class let us keep our code platform-independent, meaning it will work on both Windows and Unix-based platforms. In a Unix-based platform such as Ubuntu and MacOS the Path class returns a PosixPath object, while on Windows it returns WindowsPath. You don’t need to worry about it, the Path class handles the differences between the platforms for you.
Joining paths is much more simple and intuitive than with os.path.join, using only the / operator to join paths:
An absolute path can be generated by:
You can always convert Path object back to a string using casting:

title: pathlib — a Better Way to Work with Paths in Python
text:
Extract Components of a Path
The Path object can also help us to get different components of the full path.
Get the file name (without extension):
path_to_my_file.stem

# 'my_file'
Get the file name (with extension):
path_to_my_file.name

# 'my_file.txt'
Get only the extension:
path_to_my_file.suffix

# '.txt'
Get the parent directory as another Path object:
path_to_file = Path('/home/my_user/my_file.txt')
path_to_file.parent

# PosixPath('/home/my_user')
Get the base path (before the directories):
path_to_file.anchor

# '/' on linux
# 'C:\\' on Windows
Get all parts as a tuple:
path_to_file.parts

# ('/', 'home', 'my_user', 'my_file.txt')

title: pathlib — a Better Way to Work with Paths in Python
section: Create, Remove, and Change Files and Directories
text:
Create, Remove, and Change Files and Directories
A file can be removed by:
path_to_my_file.unlink(missing_ok=True)
if the missing_ok flag is set to True an error will not be raised if the file doesn’t exist.
We can now check if the file exists (that also works for directories):
path_to_my_file.exists()

# False
Other methods we can use to check files and directories are:
path_to_my_file.is_file()

# False

path_to_my_file.is_dir()

# False

path_to_my_file.parent.is_dir()

# True
Now let’s recreate the file and write text to it:
path_to_my_file.touch(exist_ok=True)
path_to_my_file.write_text('Hello')
if the exist_ok flag is set to True an error will not be raised if the file exists.
To read the content:
print(path_to_my_file.read_text())

# Hello
To rename a file, we need to create a new path with the new name. We can use the with_stem method to replace the name of the file (without the extension) and then rename the file:
new_name_path = path_to_my_file.with_stem('new_file')
path_to_my_file.rename(new_name_path)
We can also change the extension:
new_suffix = new_name_path.with_suffix('.md')
new_name_path.replace(new_suffix)
Creating a directory can be done using mkdir:
new_dir_path = path_to_my_file.parent / 'new_dir'
new_dir_path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
where the parents flag, if set to True will also create the intermediate directories.
To remove the last child directory:
new_dir_path.rmdir()

title: pathlib — a Better Way to Work with Paths in Python
text:
List Files by Pattern
Finally, we can use the glob method to search for files by pattern inside a directory:
current_dir = Path.cwd()
txt_files = current_dir.glob('*.txt')
or, for a recursive search inside subdirectories:
txt_files = current_dir.rglob('*.txt')

title: pathlib — a Better Way to Work with Paths in Python
text:
Final Thoughts

title: Knowledge Distillation — How Networks Can Teach
text:
Source
In the rapidly advancing field of deep learning, deploying high-performance models in real-world applications often comes with a key challenge: the balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. Many state-of-the-art models are large and resource-intensive, making them impractical for deployment on devices with limited memory or processing power, such as mobile phones, embedded systems, or autonomous vehicles. This is where knowledge distillation becomes a powerful technique.
The core idea of knowledge distillation is to transfer knowledge from a large, complex model to a smaller, more efficient one without significant loss of accuracy.
This post will explore the principles behind knowledge distillation, its various techniques, and how it can be applied to deep learning models in computer vision. Let’s dive into how it works and what makes it so effective.

title: Knowledge Distillation — How Networks Can Teach
text:
Knowledge Distillation
Knowledge distillation is a technique for transferring insights from a large, complex model or group of models to a single, more compact model that is feasible for deployment in real-world scenarios with practical limitations. In essence, it serves as a method of model compression.
This technique is predominantly applied to neural network models that feature complex architectures with multiple layers and numerous parameters. While deep learning models become more successful and bigger than ever, the deployment of extensive deep neural networks poses significant challenges, particularly for edge devices that have restricted memory and computational resources. This is why knowledge distillation methods have become increasingly important for real-world implementations.
In knowledge distillation, we take advantage of the complex network and use it as a “teacher”, to help a smaller and resource-friendly “student” model to learn from it, aiming to replicate the teacher’s performance. The following section will explore the structure and mechanisms of the knowledge distillation technique in greater detail.

title: Knowledge Distillation — How Networks Can Teach
text:
How to Transfer the Knowledge
As mentioned previously, our goal is to use an intricate network with high performance (the “teacher”), to teach a small and simpler network the knowledge it needs to perform well.
When we refer to knowledge in this context, we mainly talk about the weights and biases the network learns during training. These weights and biases are responsible for the results of the networks. However, since the student network has significantly fewer parameters than the teacher, we can’t just copy the values of the teacher parameters to the student. We need a way to transfer the knowledge to the student.
There are three techniques to transfer the knowledge.

Response-based
This is the most straightforward and commonly used method in knowledge distillation. It focuses on training the student model to replicate the final output predictions of the teacher model. This approach uses the prediction (or “response”) of the teacher as the primary source of knowledge to transfer to the student.



The generic response-based knowledge distillation. Source.




Feature-based
This type of knowledge distillation extends the knowledge transfer process beyond just the final outputs of the teacher model to include the internal feature representations learned by the teacher. This approach aims to make the student model learn the intermediate representations (the feature maps) that the teacher extracts from the input data, providing a deeper level of guidance.



The generic feature-based knowledge distillation. Source.




Relation-based
This type of distillation method focuses on transferring knowledge about the relations among data samples, layers, or feature representations from the teacher model to the student model. Instead of directly mimicking the teacher’s outputs or internal features, relation-based distillation trains the student to capture the relationships between multiple feature representations or data points learned by the teacher, such as correlations, similarities, embedding, or probabilistic distributions.



Generic relation-based knowledge distillation. Source.

title: Knowledge Distillation — How Networks Can Teach
text:
Distillation Schemes
There are several techniques to train the teacher and student models to perform knowledge distillation. The three main categories of knowledge distillation are offline distillation, online distillation, and self-distillation.
Offline distillation is the most popular. We first train the large teacher model, and after that, we use the pre-trained teacher to train the small student model. In the online distillation case, we train the teacher and the student simultaneously, so it is not a two-step process like the offline one, but an end-to-end training. Self-distillation is a special case of online distillation where the same network is used for both the teacher and student. An example of such a technique is where knowledge from deeper sections of the network is distilled into shallow sections of it.
There is a lot more to say about knowledge distillation techniques, and you can learn more from this paper.

title: Knowledge Distillation — How Networks Can Teach
text:
Offline Response-based Knowledge Distillation
From now on we will focus on the most popular and straightforward technique of knowledge distillation, which is an offline learning of a response-based scheme.
The core idea behind it is to train a student model to approximate the results of a pre-trained teacher model. This involves several key steps:

Soft Targets: Instead of simply training the student to match the hard labels (e.g., a class label like “cat” or “dog”), like in the regular training scheme, knowledge distillation leverages the “soft targets” produced by the teacher. These soft targets are probability distributions over all possible classes (usually achieved by soft-max), and they contain information about the teacher’s confidence in its predictions.
Temperature Scaling: During distillation, the teacher’s output is often scaled by a temperature parameter. The teacher’s predictions become softer by setting a higher temperature, which helps the student learn from subtle relationships between classes. For example, if an image has a high probability of both “dog” and “wolf,” this hint from the teacher helps the student understand that these classes are visually similar, thus improving its generalization.
Loss Function: Knowledge distillation involves a special loss function that combines two terms: one that aligns the student’s predictions with the hard ground truth labels (the one true label of the image, like “dog”) as in regular training, and another that aligns the student’s predictions with the teacher’s soft targets (which give each class a probability). By optimizing this combined loss, the student learns from the ground truth and the teacher’s nuanced output, allowing it to approximate the teacher’s performance more closely.

title: Knowledge Distillation — How Networks Can Teach
text:
Let’s Code It
In this part, we will implement a simple knowledge-distillation scheme using offline response-based learning. We will use a large network as the teacher, and a smaller version as a student.
The full notebook can be found here.
We start by importing all the necessary modules and setting a device to use.
from copy import deepcopy
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
import torchvision.transforms.v2 as transforms
import torchvision.datasets as datasets

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
torch.manual_seed(42)
We will use the CIFAR-10 dataset, which contains RGB images of size 32x32 for ten classes.



A sample of images from the CIFAR-10 dataset. Source: https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~kriz/cifar.html


We will use torchvision to download and use the dataset and to define a transformation that converts the images to PyTorch tensors.
transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.ToTensor()
])

train_dataset = datasets.CIFAR10(root='data', train=True, download=True, transform=transform)
test_dataset = datasets.CIFAR10(root='data', train=False, download=True, transform=transform)
We use the datasets to create DataLoader objects.
train_loader = DataLoader(train_dataset, batch_size=128, shuffle=True, num_workers=2)
test_loader = DataLoader(test_dataset, batch_size=128, shuffle=False, num_workers=2)
After having the data, we can define the models. Let’s start with the teacher model, which will be a CNN model with a classifier.
class TeacherModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.features_extractor = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(3, 128, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(128),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(128, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(64),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2),
            nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(64),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(64, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(32),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2),
        )

        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(2048, 512),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Dropout(0.1),
            nn.Linear(512, num_classes)
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.features_extractor(x)
        x = torch.flatten(x, 1)
        x = self.classifier(x)
        return x
And the student model.
class StudentModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.features_extractor = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(3, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(16),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2),
            nn.Conv2d(16, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(16),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2),
        )

        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(1024, 256),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Dropout(0.1),
            nn.Linear(256, num_classes)
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.features_extractor(x)
        x = torch.flatten(x, 1)
        x = self.classifier(x)
        return x
As you can see, the student model is shallower and narrower than the teacher model but has a similar architecture.
We want a training function and also a test function to measure accuracy.
def train(model, dataloader, epochs, learning_rate, device):
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)

    model.to(device)
    model.train()

    for epoch in range(epochs):
        running_loss = 0.0
        for images, labels in dataloader:
            images = images.to(device)
            labels = labels.to(device)

            optimizer.zero_grad()
            outputs = model(images)

            loss = criterion(outputs, labels)
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()

            running_loss += loss.item()

        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs}, Mean Loss: {running_loss / len(dataloader)}")
def test(model, data_loader, device):
    model.to(device)
    model.eval()

    correct = 0
    total = 0

    with torch.no_grad():
        for images, labels in data_loader:
            images = images.to(device)
            labels = labels.to(device)

            outputs = model(images)
            predicted_class = torch.argmax(outputs, dim=1)

            total += labels.size(0)
            correct += (predicted_class == labels).sum().item()

    accuracy = 100 * correct / total
    print(f"Test Accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}%")
    return accuracy
Now we create instances of the teacher models, and of the student model, and train them regularly. We also clone the student model to use later with knowledge distillation.
print('Teacher')
teacher = TeacherModel(num_classes=10)
train(teacher, train_loader, epochs=30, learning_rate=0.001, device=device)
test_accuracy_teacher = test(teacher, test_loader, device)

print('\nStudent')
student1 = StudentModel(num_classes=10)
student2 = deepcopy(student1)
train(student1, train_loader, epochs=30, learning_rate=0.001, device=device)
test_accuracy_student1 = test(student1, test_loader, device)
Teacher
Epoch 1/30, Mean Loss: 1.227013551975455
Epoch 2/30, Mean Loss: 0.8006297277520075
.
.
.
Epoch 30/30, Mean Loss: 0.042777400205383447
Test Accuracy: 80.35%

Student
Epoch 1/30, Mean Loss: 1.3870741598441472
Epoch 2/30, Mean Loss: 1.0735777561621898
.
.
.
Epoch 30/30, Mean Loss: 0.19093702329546594
Test Accuracy: 68.70%
As we can see, the teacher model performs better than the student model. Now, we want to use knowledge distillation to see if it improves the student’s performance. First, we define a new training function that uses the teacher’s result for the training of the student.
def train_knowledge_distillation(teacher, student, data_loader, epochs, learning_rate, temperature, alpha, device):
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    criterion_distill = nn.KLDivLoss(reduction='batchmean')
    optimizer = optim.Adam(student.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)
    teacher.to(device)
    student.to(device)
    teacher.eval()
    student.train()

    for epoch in range(epochs):
        running_loss = 0.0
        for images, labels in data_loader:
            images = images.to(device)
            labels = labels.to(device)

            optimizer.zero_grad()

            # Forward pass with the teacher model
            with torch.no_grad():
                teacher_logits = teacher(images)

            # Forward pass with the student model
            student_logits = student(images)

            # Calculate the soft label loss
            soft_targets = torch.softmax(teacher_logits / temperature, dim=1)
            soft_probs = torch.log_softmax(student_logits / temperature, dim=1)

            distillation_loss = criterion_distill(soft_probs, soft_targets)

            # Calculate the true label loss
            label_loss = criterion(student_logits, labels)

            # Weighted sum of the two losses
            loss = alpha * label_loss + (1.0 - alpha) * temperature**2 * distillation_loss
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()

            running_loss += loss.item()

        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs}, Loss: {running_loss / len(data_loader)}")
Most of the function is identical to the previous function, but we add a distillation loss term that uses soft labels based on the teacher results. This loss uses KL divergence (Kullback–Leibler divergence), which measures how much a model distribution is different from a true distribution. In our case, we assume the probability for each class that the teacher produces is the target probability, and we want to measure the differences between the probabilities the student gives and the teacher’s result. Pay attention that PyTorch KLDivLoss assumes the input is in a log scale (but the target doesn’t have to), so we use log_softmax on the student’s logits. You can also see that we use a temperature term to smooth the probabilities that the softmax produces.
\[
p(z_i, T) = \frac{\exp(z_i / T)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j / T)}
\]
In addition, we also calculate the regular cross-entropy loss with the true labels. The total loss can be written as:
\[
\mathcal{L} = \alpha \mathcal{L}_{\text{hard}} + (1 - \alpha) T^2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{soft}}
\]
where the hard loss is a cross-entropy with the real labels, the soft loss is the KL divergence on the smoothed probabilities, \(T\) is the temperature we have used for the smoothed probabilities, and \(\alpha\) is a weight parameter.
Now we can train the clone of the student with the new procedure. It’s important to notice that the clone is identical to the original student model before the training.
train_knowledge_distillation(teacher, student2, train_loader, epochs=30, learning_rate=0.001, temperature=2, alpha=0.8, device=device)
test_accuracy_student_with_distillation = test(student2, test_loader, device)
Epoch 1/30, Loss: 2.1964448251382773
Epoch 2/30, Loss: 1.6716872932356033
.
.
.
Epoch 30/30, Loss: 0.3442998861946413
Test Accuracy: 71.08%
You can see we achieve a nice improvement by only adding information from the teacher model.

title: Knowledge Distillation — How Networks Can Teach
text:
Conclusion
Knowledge distillation offers a practical and effective way to bridge the gap between state-of-the-art performance and real-world constraints. By transferring the knowledge from a large, complex model to a smaller, more efficient one, developers can deploy their systems on resource-limited devices without sacrificing accuracy. We saw various methods to use the knowledge distillation idea, and in the example we explored, we demonstrated how a teacher-student framework can be implemented, showcasing the simplicity and effectiveness of applying this method in computer vision tasks. As AI continues to evolve, techniques like knowledge distillation will remain essential for enabling advanced models to perform efficiently in resource-constrained environments.

title: Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 1
text:
This post is part of a series of posts about diffusion models:
The field of image generative models is highly developed. A lot of great models have been introduced in recent years, such as AutoEncoders, Variational AutoEncoder, and, of course, the Generative Adversarial Network. In most of the models, we train a network to take some noise and output a new image. In some of the models, we can even add to the noise some conditions of our own to direct the model to the results we want.
Usually, those networks go from noise to image in one step (or, to be more exact, in one forward pass). That means the network has hard work to understand how to convert the noise to a fine image, which can lead to blurred results and some artifacts. If the network makes an error, it can not be fixed, and we see it in the final image.
Although the models improve all the time, and nowadays we can get very high quality images using the types of models mentioned above, it could be very beneficial if we wouldn’t need to generate the image in one forward pass but iteratively improve it step by step. In this way, even if the model makes some mistakes, it has the opportunity to find and correct these mistakes in the later steps.
On the basis of this idea, enters the diffusion models. Diffusion models are relatively new, but their origins appeared already in 2015 in the paper “Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics”. Diffusion-based models achieve phenomenal results, and you probably saw some images produced by models like DALL-E 2 by OpenAI and Imagen by Google.
Diffusion models use many steps to generate the final image. In each step, the model makes a refinement of the result of the previous step. In this way, the model can gradually improve the result, get a better image after each step, and also fix errors that are made along the way.

title: Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 1
text:
Diffusion Models Key Idea
The key idea of the diffusion models is to remove the noise from the image gradually. We start with a completely noisy image, and we want to denoise it. We can think of that noise image as the target image that is corrupted by adding a little Gaussian noise (for example) over many steps. The network goal is to understand how this noise was added so that it can remove it. In each step, the network removes some noise to find a less noisy version of the target image and then uses this image as the input, and it tries to remove a little bit more noise, and so on, until we get a fine image.



Graphical description of the diffusion model. In each step, a little bit of noise is removed. Image from the paper “Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models”


The following gif illustrates the process of the diffusion model:



Illustration of the reverse process of a diffusion model. The model starts from a complete noise image, and then, step by step, it removes the noise until it gets a clean image.


The training of a diffusion model consists of two main parts:

Forward process — the process of adding noise to the image until it becomes a pure noise image. We can control the process by choosing the number of steps, how much noise is added in each step, what type of noise we add, and what is the distribution parameters of the noise (for example, we can select Gaussian noise with some mean and variance that can also be changed between steps).
Reverse process — the process where the model learns how to denoise the image gradually. This process starts with a complete noise image and should finish with a good looking image.

In the next part, we will go over the processes in more detail and formulate them mathematically. We understand how to sample the noise in the different steps and how the model can be trained to predict the noise it should remove from the image.

title: Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 6
text:
In this post, we are going to focus on sampling from the reverse process.
This post is part of a series of posts about diffusion models:

Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 1
Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 2
Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 3
Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 4
Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 5
Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 6 (this post)
Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 7
Full implementation

When our model will be fully trained (and even during the training), we will want to reconstruct images using the reverse process. For that, we are going to implement Algorithm 2 from the DDPM paper for sampling from the reverse process and get a new image, which hopefully looks like it comes from the real distribution.



Algorithm 2 from the  DDPM paper 


This algorithm describes the reverse process we discussed in parts 2 and 3. We start with a pure standard Gaussian noise, and we gradually denoise it using the prediction of our model. In the end, we get \(\mathbf{x}_0\), which should be a clean image from the real distribution. At each step, we try to predict \(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\) based on the expressions we derivate in parts 2 and 3, such as
\[p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{t-1} | \mathbf{x}_t) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}; \boldsymbol{\mu}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t))\]
\[\boldsymbol{\mu}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}} \left( \mathbf{x}_t - \frac{1 - \alpha_t}{\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t) \right)\]
\[\mathbf{x}_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_1}} (\mathbf{x}_1 - \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_1} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_1}} (\mathbf{x}_1 - \sqrt{1 - \alpha_1} \boldsymbol{\epsilon})\]
\[\boldsymbol{\mu}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_1, 1) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_1}} \left( \mathbf{x}_1 - \frac{1 - \alpha_1}{\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_1}} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_1, 1) \right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_1}} \left( \mathbf{x}_1 - \frac{1 - \alpha_1}{\sqrt{1 - \alpha_1}} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_1, 1) \right)\]
Note that the variance we use in the process is known; we don’t need to predict it.
We start by implementing a basic sampling from \(p\)
@torch.no_grad()
def sample_p(model, x_t, t, clipping=True):
  """
  Sample from p_θ(xₜ₋₁|xₜ) to get xₜ₋₁ according to Algorithm 2
  """
  betas_t_sampled = sample_by_t(betas_t, t, x_t.shape)
  sqrt_1_minus_alphas_bar_t_sampled = sample_by_t(sqrt_1_minus_alphas_bar_t, t, x_t.shape)
  one_over_sqrt_alphas_t_sampled = sample_by_t(one_over_sqrt_alphas_t, t, x_t.shape)

  if clipping:
    sqrt_alphas_bar_t_sampled = sample_by_t(sqrt_alphas_bar_t, t, x_t.shape)
    sqrt_alphas_bar_t_minus_1_sampled = sample_by_t(sqrt_alphas_bar_t_minus_1, t, x_t.shape)
    alphas_bar_t_sampled = sample_by_t(alphas_bar_t, t, x_t.shape)
    sqrt_alphas_t_sampled = sample_by_t(sqrt_alphas_t, t, x_t.shape)
    alphas_bar_t_minus_1_sampled = sample_by_t(alphas_bar_t_minus_1, t, x_t.shape)

    x0_reconstruct = 1 / sqrt_alphas_bar_t_sampled * (x_t - sqrt_1_minus_alphas_bar_t_sampled * model(x_t, t))
    x0_reconstruct = torch.clip(x0_reconstruct, -1., 1.)
    predicted_mean = (sqrt_alphas_bar_t_minus_1_sampled * betas_t_sampled) / (1 - alphas_bar_t_sampled) * x0_reconstruct + (sqrt_alphas_t_sampled * (1 - alphas_bar_t_minus_1_sampled)) /  (1 - alphas_bar_t_sampled) * x_t

  else:
    predicted_mean = one_over_sqrt_alphas_t_sampled * (x_t - betas_t_sampled / sqrt_1_minus_alphas_bar_t_sampled * model(x_t, t))

  if t[0].item() == 1:
    return predicted_mean
  else:
    posterior_variance_sampled = sample_by_t(posterior_variance, t, x_t.shape)
    noise = torch.randn_like(x_t)
    return predicted_mean + torch.sqrt(posterior_variance_sampled) * noise
The function above is not part of the training, so we wrap it with the torch.no_grad() decorator. Pay attention that there are two modes of implementation here: with and without clipping. The version without the clipping is exactly as in Algorithm 2. However, when we reconstruct \(\mathbf{x}_0\), it should be in the range \([-1, 1]\), and that is the reason for the clipping. While the training could perform well without the clipping for simple training datasets, it is better to use the clipping. The expression for the mean in the clipping mode we use is the one we got in part 3:
\[\mu_t(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{x}_0) = \frac{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}\beta_t}{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}\mathbf{x}_0 + \frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1 - \bar{\alpha}_{t-1})}{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}\mathbf{x}_t\]
and the reconstruction of \(\mathbf{x}_0\) is followed by the expression from part 3:
\[\mathbf{x}_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}} (\mathbf{x}_t - \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t} \boldsymbol{\epsilon})\]
Now, we can implement the full Algorithm 2 with a function that lets us sample images from the reverse process.
from tqdm import tqdm
@torch.no_grad()
def sampling(model, shape, image_noise_steps_to_keep=1):
  """
  Implementing Algorithm 2 - sampling.
  Args:
    model (torch.Module): the model that predict the noise
    shape (tuple): shape of the data (batch, channels, image_size, image_size)
  Returns:
    (list): list containing the images in the different steps of the reverse process
  """

  batch = shape[0]
  images = torch.randn(shape, device=device)  # pure noise
  images_list = []

  for timestep in tqdm(range(num_timesteps, 0, -1), desc='sampling timestep'):
    images = sample_p(model, images, torch.full((batch,), timestep, device=device, dtype=torch.long))
    if timestep <= image_noise_steps_to_keep:
      images_list.append(images.cpu())
  return images_list

title: Markov Chain Monte Carlo — or How to Estimate Unknown Probability Function
text:
In the field of probability and statistics, it is not uncommon to encounter situations where the probability distribution function cannot be calculated directly. One example of such a situation is the Bayesian inference.
A popular example of Bayesian inference is the estimation of model parameters. The parameters are the elements that define the model structure. For example, for a normal distribution, the parameters are the mean and the variance. For an exponential distribution, the parameter is \(\lambda\).
In this case, we usually have some samples \(x\) that come from a distribution with unknown parameters \(\theta\), but we assume we have some prior knowledge about \(\theta\) we can express using a probability function \(p(\theta)\). Using Bayes theorem, we can find the probability for \(\theta\) according to observed data \(x\).
\[
p(\theta\vert{}x) = \frac{p(x\vert{}\theta)p(\theta)}{p(x)}
\]
In most cases, the calculation of the numerator is not too difficult. However, the normalization factor can be a challenge. To find \(p(x)\), we usually need to calculate the integral
\[
p(x) = \int_{\theta} p(x\vert{}\theta)p(\theta)d\theta
\]
In some simple cases (especially in low dimensions), we can compute that integral, but in higher dimensions, it may become intractable. So, instead of computing \(p(\theta\vert{}x)\) directly, we need to use some approximation.
There are two main approaches to tackling this problem. The first one is the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which is based on sampling from the unknown distribution, and we are going to deal with in this post. The second one is the Variational Inference, which is an approximation-based approach.
Before we continue, if you want to recall what Markov Chain and Monte Carlo are, you can read about them in my previous posts here and here.

title: Markov Chain Monte Carlo — or How to Estimate Unknown Probability Function
text:
Markov Chain Monte Carlo
As described earlier, we have some unknown probability density function (\(p(\theta\vert{}x)\)) we know up to a normalization factor (\(p(x)\)). That means we have some unknown distribution function \(q(x)\) and some known distribution \(f(x)\) such that \(q(x) \propto f(x)\). We want to sample from the unknown distribution so we can estimate it. In the MCMC approach, we want to sample a new data point in a way that depends on the previous sample. The concept of a new state based only on the previous step is the main idea of the Markov Chain. The Monte Carlo part comes from the simulated sampling from the unknown distribution.
Our final goal is to construct a Markov Chain that eventually describes the unknown distribution. But how can we do that? We need a Markov Chain whose stationary state is \(q(x)\). In such a case, sampling using the Markov Chain (from the point it gets to the stationary state) is exactly like sampling from \(q(x)\) for all the next steps of the chain.
To show we get to a stationary state, we want to check the detailed balance equation:
\[
q(x)T(y\vert{}x) = q(y)T(x\vert{}y) \qquad \forall x, y
\]
The equation says that the probability of transition to go from the state \(x\) to the state \(y\) multiplied by the probability of being in the state \(x\) is equal to the probability of transition to go from the state \(y\) to the state \(x\) multiplied by the probability of being in the state \(y\), for all \(x\) and \(y\) (where \(T\) can be thought of as a transition matrix). If that equation is true for all \(x\) and \(y\), we can sum it over all the states so
\[
\sum_i q(x_i)T(y\vert{}x_i) = \sum_i q(y)T(x_i\vert{}y) = q(y) \sum_i T(x_i\vert{}y) = q(y)
\]
The last equation is true because the sum of all the transition probabilities from a state in a Markov chain is equal to \(1\). Remember also that the equation is true for every \(y\). The equation above describes the stationary condition of a Markov chain:
\[
\pi T = \pi
\]
When we multiply a state vector \(\pi\) (which is a row vector) with the transition matrix \(T\) of the Markov chain in the stationary state, we get the same state vector. Look at the first element of \(\pi\) on the right-hand side, \(\pi_1\), for example. According to the equation above, it equals to
\[
\pi_1 = \sum_i \pi_i T_{i,1}
\]
where \(T_{i,1}\) is the transition probability to move from state \(i\) to state \(1\), \(T(1\vert{}i)\). This is exactly like the equation we saw before, so it truly describes a stationary state condition.
If we can prove the detailed balance condition, we can show we are in a stationary state that describes the probability function we want to find.
But there is another thing we need to take care of. If our Markov chain has a stationary state, it won’t get to it immediately. We need to take many steps before we move to the stationary state. So, when we start to take steps in our chain, we want to “burn” the first steps before we actually take samples. This first stage is called “burn-in”.





All we have discussed up until now is the general idea of the MCMC method — construct a Markov chain with a stationary state that describes the unknown probability and sample from it. Now, we are going to see an implementation of this general idea as a specific algorithm called the Metropolis—Hastings algorithm.

title: Markov Chain Monte Carlo — or How to Estimate Unknown Probability Function
text:
Metropolis — Hastings Algorithm
The first thing we need to define is an easier distribution we can sample new data from, where each new sample data depends on the previous data point (that’s the Markovian property). For example, we can choose to work with a normal distribution with a mean equal to the previous sample.
\[
g(x_{t+1}\vert{}x_t) = \mathcal{N}(x_t, \sigma^2)
\]
Using this distribution \(g\), we generate a new candidate point we can accept as a new sample from the unknown distribution or reject. For accepting or rejecting, we want to define an acceptance probability \(A\) to move from the point \(x_t\) to the new candidate \(x_{t+1}\). For defining \(A\), we want to use the detailed balance condition:
\[
q(x)T(y\vert{}x) = q(y)T(x\vert{}y) \qquad \forall x, y
\]
and remember that \(q(x) = f(x) / C\) where \(C\) is some normalization constant. Let’s focus on the transition probability \(T\). To move from state \(x\) to state \(y\), we need our \(g\) distribution to generate \(y\) (where the previous state was \(x\)) and also to accept this transition. We can write the detailed balance condition as:
\[
\frac{f(x)}{C} g(y\vert{}x) A(x \rightarrow y) = \frac{f(y)}{C} g(x\vert{}y) A(y \rightarrow x)
\]
We can simplify the above equation as
\[
\frac{A(x \rightarrow y)}{A(y \rightarrow x)} = \underbrace{\frac{f(y)}{f(x)}}_{r_f} \underbrace{\frac{g(x\vert{}y)}{g(y\vert{}x)}}_{r_g}
\]
The algorithm defines the acceptance probability as follows
\[
A(x \rightarrow y) = \begin{cases} r_f r_g, & \text{if } r_f r_g < 1 \\ 1, & \text{if } r_f r_g \geq 1 \end{cases}
\]
\[
A(y \rightarrow x) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } r_f r_g < 1 \\ \frac{1}{r_f r_g}, & \text{if } r_f r_g \geq 1 \end{cases}
\]
Or simply
\[
A(x \rightarrow y) = \min(1, r_f r_g)
\]
If we accept the candidate, the next state of the Markov chain is the new candidate, but if we do not accept it, the next state will simply be the previous state.
To better understand this, let’s assume \(g\) is indeed a normal distribution with mean as the previous state and variance \(\sigma^2\), as we suggested earlier. In this case, \(g(x\vert{}y)\) is the same as \(g(y\vert{}x)\) since the normal distribution is symmetric.



In blue, a normal distribution with a mean of -1 and variance of 2, and in orange, a normal distribution with a mean of 1 and variance of 2. The probability density of 1 for the blue distribution is the same as that of -1 for the orange one because of the symmetry of the normal distribution.


In such a case, the value of \(r_g\) is \(1\), and so the acceptance probability is
\[
A(x \rightarrow y) = \min(1, r_f) = \min\left(1, \frac{f(y)}{f(x)}\right) = \min\left(1, \frac{q(y)}{q(x)}\right)
\]
So if the probability of getting \(y\), \(q(y)\), is greater than that of getting \(x\), we want to move to \(y\) and \(A\) is \(1\). We move to the area of high probability to get more samples from that area. But if the probability of \(x\), the current state, is greater than \(y\) there is some probability of moving to that state, which is in the area of a lower probability. As the new state \(y\) is smaller relative to \(x\), the probability of moving to it gets lower. This behavior ensures we get more samples for the high probability area and better describe the real unknown probability function.

title: Markov Chain Monte Carlo — or How to Estimate Unknown Probability Function
text:
Let’s Code It
After understanding the Metropolis—Hastings algorithm, let’s see a code example to understand it better.
We are going to use the following density function \(f(x)\)
\[
f(x) = \begin{cases} e^{-(x+2)^2}, & \text{if } x < 0 \\ e^{-(x-3)^4}, & \text{if } x \geq 0 \end{cases}
\]
To make it a probability density function \(q(x)\), we need to find its normalization factor. For that, we can use WolframAlpha and find the normalization factor to be \(3.58111\). In the same way, we can find the expectation value of \(q(x)\) and get \(0.5284\). Moreover, we are going to use a normal distribution function for the function \(g(x)\).
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def f(x):
  if isinstance(x,float):
    x = np.array([x])
  results = np.zeros_like(x, dtype=float)
  less_than_zero = x < 0
  results[less_than_zero] = np.exp(-(x[less_than_zero] + 2) ** 2)
  results[~less_than_zero] = np.exp(-(x[~less_than_zero] - 3) ** 4)
  return results

# normal PDF
def g(x, mu, sigma_2):
    return 1 / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi * sigma_2) * np.exp(-0.5 * (x-mu) ** 2 / sigma_2)

C = 3.58111
EXPECTATION = 1.8926 / C # = 0.5284
Let’s look at how the distributions \(f(x)\) and \(q(x)\) look like.
x_points = np.linspace(-6 , 6 , 1000)
f_distribution = f(x_points)
q_distribution = f_distribution / C

plt.plot(x_points, f_distribution, label='f(x)')
plt.plot(x_points, q_distribution, label='q(x)')
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('density')
plt.legend()





Now, we run the algorithm itself
num_of_samples = int(5e6)
num_of_accepted = 0
samples = np.zeros(num_of_samples)
var = 4

for ii in range(num_of_samples-1):
  candidate = np.random.normal(samples[ii], var)
  A_prob = min(1, f(candidate) / f(samples[ii]))

  if np.random.random() < A_prob:
    samples[ii+1] = candidate
    num_of_accepted += 1
  else:
    samples[ii+1] = samples[ii]
We make 5 million samples. At each iteration, we get a candidate according to the previous step using \(g(x)\) with the mean as the previous sample and a variance of \(4\). Then, we calculate the acceptance probability \(A\), and according to it, we decide if we take the candidate as the next state or use the previous step.
Next, we want to remove the burn-in part from the sampling data.
burn_in = 1000
samples_to_use = samples[burn_in:]
We can check the percentage of the sample we accepted.
print(f"Acceptances: {num_of_accepted / num_of_samples * 100:.2f}%")
# Acceptances: 29.72%
Let’s compare the sampling distribution to the real one \(q(x)\).
plt.hist(samples_to_use, bins=200, density=True)
plt.plot(x_points, q_distribution, label='q(x)')
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('density')
plt.legend()





We see a good match between the sampling distribution and the real distribution \(q(x)\). We can also compute the mean.
samples_to_use.mean()
#  0.532
This result is close to the real one.
One problem this algorithm has is a high correlation between the samples since the next sample is strongly related to the previous one. Let’s check the correlation of the samples.
from scipy.stats import pearsonr
plt.scatter(samples_to_use[:-1], samples_to_use[1:], s=1)
plt.xlabel('Previous Sample')
plt.ylabel('Current Sample')
corr = np.round(pearsonr(samples_to_use[:-1], samples_to_use[1:])[0], 2)
plt.title(f'Correlation = {corr}')





A correlation of \(0.82\) is pretty high. We can reduce this correlation if we take each 10th sample, for example.
samples_to_use_no_correlation = samples_to_use[::10]
plt.hist(samples_to_use_no_correlation, bins=200, density=True)
plt.plot(x_points, q_distribution, label='q(x)')
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('density')
plt.legend()





samples_to_use_no_correlation.mean()
#  0.536
plt.scatter(samples_to_use_no_correlation[:-1], samples_to_use_no_correlation[1:], s=1)
plt.xlabel('Previous Sample')
plt.ylabel('Current Sample')
corr = np.round(pearsonr(samples_to_use_no_correlation[:-1], samples_to_use_no_correlation[1:])[0], 2)
plt.title(f'Correlation = {corr}')





We see we succeeded in reducing the correlation and still keep a good distribution.

title: Migrating from Pandas to Polars: A Comprehensive Guide
text:
Introduction
Pandas has been the go-to library for data manipulation in Python for over a decade. It is powerful, flexible, and widely used in data science, machine learning, and analytics. However, as datasets grow in size, Pandas often struggles with performance due to its reliance on single-threaded execution and memory-intensive operations.
Polars, a relatively new DataFrame library, aims to address these limitations. Built using Rust, Polars is designed for speed and efficiency. It offers multi-threaded execution, a powerful query engine, and memory-efficient operations, making it an excellent alternative to Pandas for large-scale data processing.
In this post, we will explore the key advantages of Polars over Pandas and demonstrate how to migrate common Pandas operations to Polars.

title: Migrating from Pandas to Polars: A Comprehensive Guide
text:
Why Polars?

1. Performance
Polars leverages Rust and Arrow memory format to enable lightning-fast computations. It is optimized for multi-threading, allowing it to outperform Pandas significantly on large datasets.


2. Memory Efficiency
Unlike Pandas, which often requires large amounts of memory, Polars employs zero-copy operations and efficient memory layouts, reducing RAM usage considerably.


3. Lazy Execution
Polars supports lazy execution, which allows it to optimize query plans before execution, making it better for complex operations on big data.


4. Better API Design
Polars enforces stricter data types and provides a more functional API, reducing common issues like unintended type conversions and silent data corruption.
Now, let’s dive into how to migrate common Pandas operations to Polars.

title: Migrating from Pandas to Polars: A Comprehensive Guide
text:
Migrating from Pandas to Polars

1. Installation
Before we start, install Polars using:
pip install polars
Then, import the libraries:
import pandas as pd
import polars as pl


2. Creating DataFrames
Pandas
df_pd = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"],
    "age": [25, 30, 35],
    "salary": [50000, 60000, 70000]
})
Polars
df_pl = pl.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"],
    "age": [25, 30, 35],
    "salary": [50000, 60000, 70000]
})


3. Data Inspection
Pandas
df_pd.info()
df_pd.describe()
Polars
df_pl.schema  # Shows data types
df_pl.describe()
Polars’ .schema replaces .info() and .describe() provides statistical summaries.


4. Selecting Columns
Pandas
df_pd["name"]
df_pd[["name", "salary"]]
Polars
df_pl["name"]  # Series output
df_pl.select(["name", "salary"])  # DataFrame output
In Polars, .select() is preferred for multi-column selection.


5. Filtering Rows
Pandas
df_pd[df_pd["age"] > 28]
Polars
df_pl.filter(pl.col("age") > 28)
Polars uses expressions like pl.col("age") for filtering.


6. Adding New Columns
Pandas
df_pd["bonus"] = df_pd["salary"] * 0.1
Polars
df_pl = df_pl.with_columns((pl.col("salary") * 0.1).alias("bonus"))
Polars uses .with_columns() to add new columns.


7. Applying Functions
Applying the following function on the salary column.
def categorize_salary(salary):
    if salary > 60000:
        return "High"
    elif salary > 50000:
        return "Medium"
    else:
        return "Low"
Pandas
df_pd["salary_category"] = df_pd["salary"].apply(categorize_salary)
Polars
df_pl = df_pl.with_columns(
    pl.when(pl.col("salary") > 60000)
    .then(pl.lit("High"))
    .when(pl.col("salary") > 50000)
    .then(pl.lit("Medium"))
    .otherwise(pl.lit("Low"))
    .alias("salary_category")
)
Polars avoids .apply() whenever possible, replacing it with efficient vectorized expressions like when().then().otherwise().


8. Grouping and Aggregations
Pandas
df_pd.groupby("age")["salary"].mean()
Polars
df_pl.group_by("age").agg(pl.col("salary").mean())
Polars’ .agg() method explicitly defines aggregations.


9. Sorting
Pandas
df_pd.sort_values(by="salary", ascending=False)
Polars
df_pl.sort("salary", descending=True)


10. Merging DataFrames
Pandas
df2_pd = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Alice", "Bob"], "department": ["HR", "Engineering"]})
df_merged = df_pd.merge(df2_pd, on="name", how="left")
Polars
df2_pl = pl.DataFrame({"name": ["Alice", "Bob"], "department": ["HR", "Engineering"]})
df_merged = df_pl.join(df2_pl, on="name", how="left")
Polars replaces .merge() with .join().


11. Handling Missing Values
Pandas
df_pd.fillna(0)
df_pd.dropna()
Polars
df_pl.fill_null(0)
df_pl.drop_nulls()
Polars uses .fill_null() instead of .fillna() and drop_nulls() instead of dropna().


12. Lazy Execution for Big Data
One of Polars’ biggest advantages is lazy execution, which optimizes query plans before execution.
lazy_df = df_pl.lazy()
lazy_df = lazy_df.filter(pl.col("salary") > 55000)
lazy_df.collect()  # Executes the query
Lazy execution helps process large datasets efficiently. Lazy operations in Polars are not in place, so you must assign the result to a new variable or overwrite the original one because .collect() returns a new DataFrame and does not modify the original LazyFrame.

title: Migrating from Pandas to Polars: A Comprehensive Guide
text:
Conclusion
Migrating from Pandas to Polars provides significant performance and efficiency gains, especially for large datasets. With multi-threading, better memory management, and an optimized query engine, Polars is a strong alternative for data manipulation.

Key Takeaways

Polars is much faster due to multi-threading and Rust optimizations.
Memory usage is lower, making it suitable for big data.
Stronger type enforcement reduces unexpected bugs.
Lazy execution optimizes queries before execution.

While Pandas remains a powerful tool for data analysis, Polars is a compelling choice for those seeking better performance. If you’re working with large-scale data, Polars might be the better solution.

title: TorchVision Transforms V2 — an Updated Library for Image Augmentation
text:
With the PyTorch 2.0 version, torchvision 0.15 also released and brought an updated and extended API for the Transforms module.
The Transforms module lets you apply a wide range of transformations to an image (such as flipping the image, scaling, rotation, cropping, changing colors, and many more), and by so augmenting the dataset we train on and improve the model’s performance.
