Up to version 0.15, the Transforms module could handle image transformations and augmentation for image classification (because it only worked on images). For tasks like object detection or segmentation (where you also have bounding boxes and masks), you needed to extend the Transforms module by yourself or use some other augmentation libraries like Albumentations.
Version 0.15 of torchvision introduced Transforms V2 with several advantages [1]:
And the best part is that the new version is fully backward compatible with the old one. If you already use the Transforms API, you can move to the new one by just changing the import line.
Transforms V2 is still considered as BETA, but it’s not expected to be changed too much and is planned to be fully stable in torchvision 0.17.

title: TorchVision Transforms V2 — an Updated Library for Image Augmentation
text:
Let’s Code It
We can make a simple example for the task of object detection. We can start with an image with some objects in it.



Photo by karsten madsen from  Pexels 


In the first step, we import the necessary libraries and read the image.
from pathlib import Path
import torch
import torchvision.transforms.v2 as tr  # importing the new transforms module
from torchvision.io import read_image
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

image_path = Path.home() / 'Downloads' / 'image.jpg'
image = read_image(str(image_path))
We want to create a function to display the image and the transformation.
def display_tensor_augmentation(tensor_image_original, tensor_image_transformed, bboxes_original=None, bboxes_transformed=None):
    if bboxes_original is not None:
        tensor_image_original = draw_bounding_boxes(tensor_image_original, bboxes_original, width=3)

    if bboxes_transformed is not None:
        tensor_image_transformed = draw_bounding_boxes(tensor_image_transformed, bboxes_transformed, width=3)


    pil_image_original = tr.ToPILImage()(tensor_image_original.cpu())
    pil_image_transformed = tr.ToPILImage()(tensor_image_transformed.cpu())

    plt.figure()
    plt.subplot(121)
    plt.imshow(pil_image_original)
    plt.axis('off')
    plt.subplot(122)
    plt.imshow(pil_image_transformed)
    plt.axis('off')
    plt.show()
For making a transformation we need to define a set of transforms. We do it exactly as in the first version.
transform = tr.Compose([
    tr.RandomResizedCrop(size=512),
    tr.RandomHorizontalFlip(1),
])
This transformation makes a random crop of the image and resizes it to \(512 \times 512\) pixels and then flips it horizontally.



The original image and the transformed one


The previous case is the simple case used for image classification where we don’t need to deal with additional information except for the image itself.
Now let’s repeat the example but this time for an object detection task where we have a list of bounding boxes in addition to the image. For the bounding boxes information, we are going to use a special type of tensor called TVTensors. The TVTensors are regular tensors (they are actually subclasses of torch.Tensor), but hold additional information. There are four types of TVTensors: Image, BoundingBoxes, Masks, and Video.
In our case, we want to use the BoundingBoxes type to define a tensor that represents bounding boxes. For that, we need to create a standard tensor of size \((N, 4)\) for the bounding boxes information, and include additional information about the format of the bounding boxes (for example top left and bottom right) and the size of the canvas (image) where the measures of the bounding boxes were taken from.
Now, when we make a transformation on the image with the bounding box, the transform sees we ask to transform bounding box data (because we use tv_tensors.BoundingBoxes type) and can handle it as needed.
boxes = tv_tensors.BoundingBoxes(
    [
        [227, 30, 1156, 742],
        [118, 551, 265, 619],
        [121, 637, 363, 766],
        [1078, 327, 1251, 557]
    ],
    format='XYXY', canvas_size=image.shape[-2:])

transformed_image, transformed_boxes = transform(image, boxes)
Notice we didn’t have to change anything. The transform function saw we wanted to apply the transformation also on the bounding boxes, and it performed it and then returned it as another output.



The original image with bounding boxes and the transformed one. Pay attention to the apple’s bounding box at the middle of the left edge of the transformed image


It looks like it worked! But, if you look carefully at the middle of the left edge of the transformed image you will notice the bounding box of the apple, even though the apple is cropped out from the image. This is a case of a degenerate bounding box, it doesn’t capture anything but still exists in our image. To remove degenerate bounding boxes we need to add to our transformation the SanitizeBoundingBoxes transformation [2].
transform = tr.Compose([
    tr.RandomResizedCrop(size=512, antialias=True),
    tr.RandomHorizontalFlip(1),
    tr.SanitizeBoundingBoxes()  # need to add this if we use crops as part of our transformation
])

transformed_data = transform({'image': image, 'boxes': boxes, 'labels': torch.arange(boxes.shape[0])})
display_tensor_augmentation(image, transformed_data['image'], boxes, transformed_data['boxes'])



The original image with bounding boxes and the transformed one


Now there is no bounding box for the apple which is cropped out from the image. Because of the default way SanitizeBoundingBoxes works, we have passed the data as a dictionary (recall that the new transforms support arbitrary input structures) and added label information.

title: TorchVision Transforms V2 — an Updated Library for Image Augmentation
text:
Conclusion
Version 2 of the Transforms API is already available, and even though it is still in BETA, it’s pretty mature, keeps compatibility with the first version, and lets us use it for more tasks like object detection and segmentation.
[1] https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/transforms.html
[2] https://pytorch.org/vision/stable/auto_examples/transforms/plot_transforms_e2e.html#sphx-glr-auto-examples-transforms-plot-transforms-e2e-py

title: Introduction to Torch Metrics
text:
Metrics are one of the most important parts of the deep learning field. When we train a deep learning model we need to track some metrics to understand if our model is good for the task. We also need metrics to compare two models and choose the better one.
There are a lot of metrics to use. If we think, for example, about image classification, we may want to know how accurate our model is. The accuracy metrics measure what is the proportion of times the model makes the correct prediction. In the classification case, we divide the number of correct classifications by the total images we try to classify.
Another popular metrics are the precision and the recall. Suppose we have a set of images and we want to classify them as “dog image” or “non-dog image”. Each classification result can be one of four:
The precision metric tells us the ratio between the true positive predictions to the total positive predictions the model makes (that means the true positive and the false positive.
\[\text{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} = \frac{TP}{\text{total positive predictions}}\]
The Recall metric tells us the ratio between the true positive predictions to the total real positive instances (the true positive and the false negative), which is the ground truth.
\[\text{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} = \frac{TP}{\text{total positive instances}} = \frac{TP}{\text{ground truth}}\]
As you can see, there are relatively simple formulas for the metrics we have seen so far, and that is true for most of the metrics, but why calculate these metrics by ourselves if there is a great library that does it for us?

title: Introduction to Torch Metrics
text:
TorchMetrics
TorchMetrics is a library by Lightning AI that works with PyTorch and helps us to calculate and track metrics. The library can handle a variety of metrics in different fields such as classification, clustering, detection, image, audio, text, and more. It also supports basic aggregation metrics such as mean, sum, minimum maximum, etc.
Using this library introduces several advantages over implementing the metrics by yourself, such as reducing boilerplate code and standardized interface and it can also help in distributed training. Moreover, if you use PyTorch Lightning, it has full integration with TorchMetrics (but of course you can use it with PyTorch).
Each metric in TorchMetrics implements three base methods:

update() : update the state of the metric to include new information
compute() : return the metric value based on the current state
reset() : reset the metric to its initial state

The metrics inherit the torch.nn.Module so it has forward() method that lets us call the metric directly. In this case, it calls the update() method and returns the value for the current input only.
As always it will be clearer if we see an example of code, so let’s code it.

title: Introduction to Torch Metrics
text:
Let’s Code It
For the example, we will base on the PyTorch example of image classification on the MNIST dataset which can be found here.
We start by importing the necessary modules.
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import torch.optim as optim
from torchvision import datasets, transforms
from torch.optim.lr_scheduler import StepLR

# import the metrics
from torchmetrics.aggregation import MeanMetric
from torchmetrics import Accuracy, Precision, Recall
and then defining the metrics.
single_epoch_mean_train_loss = MeanMetric()
single_epoch_mean_test_loss = MeanMetric()
accuracy = Accuracy(task="multiclass", num_classes=10)
precision = Precision(task="multiclass", num_classes=10)
recall = Recall(task="multiclass", num_classes=10)
For the loss, we use the mean metric to calculate the mean loss for each epoch over all the batches. We also define accuracy precision and recall metrics. Since we deal with a multiclass case with ten classes (the digits 0 to 9) we pass the arguments task="multiclass", num_classes=10 .
Now we define the network.
class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(Net, self).__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, 1)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, 1)
        self.dropout1 = nn.Dropout(0.25)
        self.dropout2 = nn.Dropout(0.5)
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(9216, 128)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(128, 10)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.conv1(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        x = self.conv2(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        x = F.max_pool2d(x, 2)
        x = self.dropout1(x)
        x = torch.flatten(x, 1)
        x = self.fc1(x)
        x = F.relu(x)
        x = self.dropout2(x)
        x = self.fc2(x)
        output = F.log_softmax(x, dim=1)
        return output
and the training and test steps.
def train(model, device, train_loader, optimizer, epoch):
    model.train()
    for batch_idx, (data, target) in enumerate(train_loader):
        data, target = data.to(device), target.to(device)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        output = model(data)
        loss = F.nll_loss(output, target)
        single_epoch_mean_train_loss.update(loss.item())
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

    print(f'Train Epoch: {epoch} \tLoss: {single_epoch_mean_train_loss.compute()}')
    single_epoch_mean_train_loss.reset()
def test(model, device, test_loader):
    model.eval()
    test_loss = 0
    correct = 0
    with torch.no_grad():
        for data, target in test_loader:
            data, target = data.to(device), target.to(device)
            output = model(data)
            loss = F.nll_loss(output, target)
            single_epoch_mean_test_loss.update(loss.item())
            pred = output.argmax(dim=1, keepdim=True).cpu()  # get the index of the max log-probability
            target = target.cpu()
            accuracy.update(pred, target.view_as(pred))
            precision.update(pred, target.view_as(pred))
            recall.update(pred, target.view_as(pred))

    print(f'Test - Mean loss: {single_epoch_mean_test_loss.compute():.4f}, ',
    f'Accuracy: {accuracy.compute():.4f}, Precision: {precision.compute():.4f} ',
    f'Recall: {recall.compute():.4f}')

    single_epoch_mean_test_loss.reset()
    accuracy.reset()
    precision.reset()
    recall.reset()
In the steps, you can see we update the states of the metrics while going over the batches, and after the loop, we compute the metrics values, print them, and finally reset them for the next time.
We don’t need to do any calculation. TorchMetrics does all the work for us.
Finally, we train the model, and during training we can see the metrics printed to the console.
    device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'

    torch.manual_seed(0)

    transform=transforms.Compose([
        transforms.ToTensor(),
        transforms.Normalize((0.1307,), (0.3081,))
        ])
    dataset1 = datasets.MNIST('./data', train=True, download=True,
                       transform=transform)
    dataset2 = datasets.MNIST('./data', train=False,
                       transform=transform)
    train_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(dataset1, batch_size=64, shuffle=True)
    test_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(dataset2, batch_size=256, shuffle=False)

    model = Net().to(device)
    optimizer = optim.Adadelta(model.parameters(), lr=1.0)

    scheduler = StepLR(optimizer, step_size=1, gamma=0.7)

    for epoch in range(1, 15):
        train(model, device, train_loader, optimizer, epoch)
        test(model, device, test_loader)
        scheduler.step()

title: Introduction to Torch Metrics
text:
Conclusion
TorchMetrics is a powerful library to handle all your metrics during the training of deep learning models. It contains a very wide variety of metrics for different tasks, and each of them can be configured in several ways to help you get the exact metric you want to track.

title: Variational Autoencoder
text:
Generative artificial intelligence is one of the most exciting fields in deep learning. Such networks can generate new data, like image text or sound, by learning the distribution the data comes from. Various generative deep learning models exist, like Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Diffusion-based networks, and Variational Autoencoders.
In this post, we are going to focus on the Variational Autoencoder model. We start by understanding why it’s useful, derivate it mathematically, and finally implement a simple network.

title: Variational Autoencoder
text:
AutoEncoder vs Variational AutoEncoder
An AutoEncoder is a network that can take an input (image in our case), \(x\), compress it to some latent representation \(z\) using an encoder, and decode it back from \(z\) to the original data \(x\) using a decoder.



The architecture of an autoencoder. An image is compressed into some latent representation and decoded back.


The aim of this model is to get the best reconstruction possible. The network has no regularization on the latent space and can do whatever is needed to get the original image back. This means we don’t really know how the latent space is constructed, and that’s why it can be very difficult for us to use the latent space to sample a new image to generate (we can only reconstruct images we already have their latent representation).
Here comes the Variational Autoencoder. Instead of using any latent space, we use some constraints to get a latent space from which we know how to sample. For example, we can ask for a latent space, which is a normal distribution similar to the standard normal distribution, and then we can sample from this distribution to decode images.



In the above figure, the encoder returns the mean and the standard deviation of a normal distribution, then we sample a latent vector \(z\), and finally, the decoder reconstructs the image from \(z\). The main difference between the autoencoder and the variational autoencoder is that the encoder in the first one returns an encoded representation of the image as a latent vector, while the second returns a distribution as the encoded version of the image, from which we can sample a latent representation.

title: Variational Autoencoder
section: The Mathematics Behind the Variational AutoEncoder
text:
The Mathematics Behind the Variational AutoEncoder
As explained, the variational autoencoder has a probabilistic approach. The decoder represents the probability distribution to get the data \(x\) given the latent representation \(z\), \(p(x|z)\). On the other hand, the encoder represents the probability distribution of the latent \(z\) given the data \(x\), \(p(z|x)\). The relation between these two distributions is given by Bayes theorem.
\[
p(z|x) = \frac{p(x|z)p(z)}{p(x)} = \frac{p(x|z)p(z)}{\int p(x|z)p(z)dz}
\]
Where \(p(z)\) is a prior distribution of \(z\) we assume, and \(p(x)\) is the distribution of the data we generally don’t know and can’t even solve the integral that defines it. That means we also can’t compute the posterior \(p(z|x)\). Instead of computing it, we can try to approximate it using a recognition model \(q_\phi(z|x)\), such as
\[q_\phi(z|x) \approx p_\theta(z|x)\]
where \(\phi\) and \(\theta\) are the parameters of a model, and \(q_\phi(z|x)\) and \(p_\theta(z|x)\) are families of distributions parameterized by \(\phi\) and \(\theta\) (at the end, we will want to find those parameters to define the best models).
To find the parameters, we need to define an optimization problem. Because we want \(q_\phi(z|x)\) to describe best the real distribution \(p_\theta(z|x)\), we can minimize the KL divergence between them.
\[
\begin{aligned}
KL(q_\phi(z|x)||p_\theta(z|x)) &= \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi} \left[ \log \frac{q_\phi(z|x)}{p_\theta(z|x)} \right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi} \left[ \log \frac{q_\phi(z|x)p_\theta(x)}{p_\theta(z, x)} \right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi} \left[ \log \frac{q_\phi(z|x)}{p_\theta(z, x)} + \log(p_\theta(x)) \right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi} \left[ \log \frac{q_\phi(z|x)}{p_\theta(z, x)} \right] + \log(p_\theta(x)) \\
&= -\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi} \left[ \log \frac{p_\theta(z, x)}{q_\phi(z|x)} \right] + \log(p_\theta(x)) \\
&= -\mathcal{L}_{\theta,\phi}(x) + \log(p_\theta(x))
\end{aligned}
\]
We can rearrange the equation so
\[\mathcal{L}_{\theta,\phi}(x) = \log(p_\theta(x)) - KL(q_\phi(z|x)||p_\theta(z|x))\] \[\Rightarrow \mathcal{L}_{\theta,\phi}(x) \le \log(p_\theta(x))\]
The inequality is true because KL divergence is a non-negative value. That means \(\mathcal{L}_{\theta,\phi}(x)\) is a lower bound of the log-likelihood of the data (also called evidence) — and this is the reason it’s called the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO). Notice that we get an equality if and only if the KL divergence part is zero, meaning the recognition model is equal to the true posterior distribution.
From what we saw, we can understand that instead of minimizing the KL divergence, we can equivalently maximize the ELBO, \(\mathcal{L}_{\theta,\phi}(x)\). We can develop the expression for the ELBO as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}_{\theta,\phi}(x) &= \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi} \left[ \log \frac{p_\theta(z, x)}{q_\phi(z|x)} \right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi} \left[ \log \frac{p_\theta(x|z)p_\theta(z)}{q_\phi(z|x)} \right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi} \left[ \log \frac{p_\theta(z)}{q_\phi(z|x)} + \log(p_\theta(x|z)) \right] \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi} [\log(p_\theta(x|z))] - KL(q_\phi(z|x)||p_\theta(z))
\end{aligned}
\]
We see that the ELBO constructs from two terms. The first term is the expectation over the likelihood of the real model. As we want to maximize it, it can be seen as a “reconstruction error” (we want to get the data that has the most likelihood given the latent representation \(z\), which should be the original data \(x\) the \(z\) came from). The second term can be seen as a regularization. As we want to maximize the ELBO, we need to keep the KL divergence small (since it is non-negative), which means we are penalized if our recognition model \(q_\phi(z|x)\) is far from the prior. This shows the trade-off between choosing a model that is more similar to the prior or a model followed by the observed data and maximizing the likelihood.

title: Variational Autoencoder
text:
Reparametrizing Trick
As explained before, the latent representation \(z\) is sampled for \(q_\phi(z|x)\), which means it is a random variable. We need to back-propagate through \(z\) to \(\phi\) to optimize our loss function, but it’s problematic since \(z\) is a random variable sampled from some distribution. Instead, we can express \(z\) using some differentiable transformation with another random variable \(\varepsilon\), \(z = g(\varepsilon, \phi, x)\). This change lets us back-propagate through \(z\) to optimize \(\phi\), as illustrated in the following figure.

title: Variational Autoencoder
text:
Let’s Code it
We are going to implement a Variational Autoencoder for the FashionMNIST dataset. The FashionMNIST dataset contains low-resolution gray-scale images of 10 fashion items such as shirts, dresses, and shoes. We want our model to generate new images similar to those in the FashionMNIST dataset.
We start by importing the relevant libraries we are going to use.
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch import nn, optim
from torch.nn import functional as F
from torchvision import datasets
from torchvision.utils import make_grid
from torchvision.transforms.transforms import ToPILImage, ToTensor
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
And defining some constant values to use.
BATCH_SIZE = 128
EPOCHS = 100
Z_DIM = 2
LEARNING_RATE = 1e-3

device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')
The next step is to get the dataset and create a data loader. We can use torchvision to load the dataset directly.
train_data = datasets.FashionMNIST('./data', train=True, download=True,
                            transform=ToTensor())
test_data = datasets.FashionMNIST('./data', train=False,
                           transform=ToTensor())

train_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(train_data,
                                           batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=True)
test_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(test_data,
                                          batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=True)
Now, we want to build the model. As we explained, the Variational Autoencoder is composed of an encoder, sampling step, and decoder. We want to implement each of them and compose them to a full model.
class Sampling(nn.Module):
  def __init__(self):
    super().__init__()

  def forward(self, z_means, z_log_vars):
      epsilon = torch.randn_like(z_means, dtype=torch.float32)
      return z_means + torch.exp(0.5 * z_log_vars) * epsilon


class Encoder(nn.Module):
  def __init__(self, latent_dim):
    super().__init__()
    self.latent_dim = latent_dim
    self.encoder = nn.Sequential(
        nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, stride=2, padding=1),
        nn.ReLU(True),
        nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, stride=2, padding=1),
        nn.ReLU(True),
        nn.Flatten(),
        nn.Linear(7 * 7 * 64, 16),
        nn.ReLU(True)
    )
    self.lin_mean = nn.Linear(16, latent_dim)
    self.lin_log_var = nn.Linear(16, latent_dim)
    self.sampling = Sampling()

  def forward(self, x):
    x = self.encoder(x)
    z_means = self.lin_mean(x)
    z_log_vars = self.lin_log_var(x)
    z = self.sampling(z_means, z_log_vars)
    return z, z_means, z_log_vars


class Decoder(nn.Module):
  def __init__(self, latent_dim):
    super().__init__()
    self.decoder = nn.Sequential(
        nn.Linear(latent_dim, 7 * 7 * 64),
        nn.ReLU(True),
        nn.Unflatten(1, (64, 7, 7)),
        nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, 64, 3, stride=2, padding=1, output_padding=1),
        nn.ReLU(True),
        nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, 32, 3, stride=2, padding=1, output_padding=1),
        nn.ReLU(True),
        nn.ConvTranspose2d(32, 1, 3, padding=1),
        nn.Sigmoid()
    )

  def forward(self, x):
    return self.decoder(x)


class VAE(nn.Module):
  def __init__(self, latent_dim):
    super().__init__()
    self.encoder = Encoder(latent_dim)
    self.decoder = Decoder(latent_dim)

  def forward(self, x):
    z, z_means, z_log_vars = self.encoder(x)
    x = self.decoder(z)
    return x.view(-1, 1, 28, 28), z_means, z_log_vars
In the sampling step, we use \(\varepsilon\) sampled from a standard normal distribution and compute \(z\) by using the parameterize trick by multiplying it with the standard division and adding the mean to get a new value sampled from another normal distribution.
For the optimization part, we developed the expression
\[\mathcal{L}_{\theta,\phi}(x) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi} [\log(p_\theta(x|z))] - KL(q_\phi(z|x)||p_\theta(z))\]
We can make it a loss by looking at \(-\mathcal{L}_{\theta,\phi}(x)\). For the KL divergence, we are going to assume the prior \(p_\theta(z)\) is a standard normal distribution (mean of 0 and variance of 1), and we also assume \(q_\phi(z|x)\) is a normal distribution. In general, these distributions are for vectors (multivariate normal distributions), but we are going to assume the covariance matrix is diagonal, meaning each value in the vector is independent of the other.
It can be shown that for such a case, the KL divergence is given by:
\[KL(\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, diag(\sigma_1^2, ..., \sigma_n^2))||\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\sigma_i^2 + \mu_i^2 - 1 - \ln(\sigma_i^2))\]
For the second term, we have said that it represents a reconstruction error. Instead of using it directly, we can select another reconstruction term, such as L1, L2, or binary cross-entropy. Here, we are going to use binary cross entropy between the reconstructed image at the end of the decoder and the original image we use as input to the encoder.
def loss_func(x_reconstruct, x, z_means, z_log_vars):
  bce = F.binary_cross_entropy(x_reconstruct, x, reduction='sum')
  kld = 0.5 * torch.sum(z_means ** 2 + torch.exp(z_log_vars) - z_log_vars - 1)

  return bce + kld
We define the training step and the test step.
def train_step(model, dataloader, loss_tracking):
  model.train()
  for batch in dataloader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    batch = batch[0].to(device)
    reconstructed_batch, mu, log_var = model(batch)
    loss = loss_func(reconstructed_batch, batch, mu, log_var)
    current_loss = loss.item()
    loss_tracking.append(current_loss) 
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

def test_step(model, dataloader, loss_tracking):
  model.eval()
  with torch.no_grad():
    for batch in dataloader:
      batch = batch[0].to(device)
      reconstructed_batch, mu, log_var = model(batch)
      loss = loss_func(reconstructed_batch, batch, mu, log_var)
      current_loss = loss.item()
      loss_tracking.append(current_loss) 
Finally, we create the model and the optimizer and train the model.
model = VAE(Z_DIM).to(device)
optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=LEARNING_RATE)

train_loss = []
test_loss = []

for epoch in range(EPOCHS):
  train_step(model, train_loader, train_loss)
  test_step(model, test_loader, test_loss)
  print(f'Epoch {epoch}; Train loss epoch mean {np.mean(train_loss[-len(train_loader):])}, Test loss epoch mean {np.mean(test_loss[-len(test_loader):])}')
After the training, we can sample new data using the decoder.
def sample(model, image_to_sample=64, nrow=8):
  with torch.no_grad():
    z = torch.randn((image_to_sample, Z_DIM)).to(device)
    samples = model.decoder(z).cpu().view(image_to_sample, 1, 28, 28)
    grid = make_grid(samples, nrow=nrow)
    return ToPILImage()(grid)

sample(model)



We can look at how different values in the latent vector \(z\) influence the results.
z0_range = np.linspace(-2, 2, 11)
z1_range = np.linspace(-2, 2, 11)
results = []

with torch.no_grad():
  for z0 in z0_range:
    for z1 in z1_range:
      results.append(model.decoder(torch.tensor([[z0, z1]], device=device, dtype=torch.float32)).view(-1, 1, 28, 28))

image = ToPILImage()(make_grid(torch.cat(results, dim=0), 11))

plt.imshow(image)
plt.xticks([2 + (28/2) + (28+2) * ii for ii in range(len(z1_range))], [f'{x:.1f}' for x in z1_range])
plt.yticks([2 + (28/2) + (28+2) * ii for ii in range(len(z0_range))], [f'{x:.1f}' for x in z0_range])
plt.xlabel(r'$z_1$')
plt.ylabel(r'$z_0$')



We can also look at the distribution of the means as the encoder sets them.
labels_map = {
0:    "T-shirt / top",
1:    "Trouser",
2:    "Pullover",
3:    "Dress",
4:    "Coat",
5:    "Sandal",
6:    "Shirt",
7:    "Sneaker",
8:    "Bag",
9:    "Ankle boot"
}

all_data = train_data.data.unsqueeze(1) / 255.
with torch.no_grad():
  _, mu, _ = model.encoder(all_data.to(device))
mu = mu.cpu().numpy()
labels = train_data.targets.numpy()

plt.scatter(mu[:,0], mu[:, 1], c=labels)
cbar = plt.colorbar(ticks = range(10))
cbar.ax.set_yticklabels([labels_map[i] for i in range(10)])
plt.xlabel(r'$\mu_0$')
plt.ylabel(r'$\mu_1$')

title: Linear Regression with Gradient Descent from Scratch
text:
Linear regression is a sort of supervised learning model that lets us find a linear relation between the data (features) and the results (labels).
Our goal while fitting a linear regression is to find the line (or hyper-plane in the general multi-dimensions case) that produces the least error between the known data and the prediction of the model.
Let’s start with the case where we have \(m\) data points, and each point has \(n\) features. For example, if we try to predict house prices, we may have data for 10 houses (this is \(m\)), and for each house, we have 3 features: size, age, and number of bedrooms (this is \(n\)). We want to find a linear model of the form:
\[
y = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x_1 + \theta_2 x_2 + \dots + \theta_n x_n
\]
where \(y\) is the label, for example, house price, \(x_i\) are the features, and the \(\theta\)s are the model parameters. We call \(\theta_0\) the bias term, and the other \(\theta\)s are the weights of the model. You can see this equation is a linear equation. We want to find the parameters that make the minimum error between the real \(y\) value and the predicted one \(\hat{y}\).
Suppose the error (or loss function) we use is the mean square error (MSE). The objective we want to minimize is
\[
\theta = \arg \min_{\theta} \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
\]
where \(e = y_i - \hat{y}_i\) is the error for the i-th data point. To find the parameters that make this expression minimal, we can derive it according to each \(\theta\) and find when it equals zero.
\[
\begin{aligned}
0 &= \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_j} \left( \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 \right) \\
&= \frac{1}{2m} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_j} \left( \sum_{i=1}^{m} (y_i - \theta_0 - \theta_1 x_{i1} - \dots - \theta_n x_{in})^2 \right) \\
&= -\frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} (y_i - \theta_0 - \theta_1 x_{i1} - \dots - \theta_n x_{in}) x_{ij}
\end{aligned}
\]
The above equation is one equation of a set of linear equations for the θs we can solve. But, it will be more convenient to write it in a matrix notation.
\[
\begin{aligned}
0 &= \frac{1}{2m} \nabla_{\mathbf{\theta}} \|\mathbf{e}\|^2 \\
&= \frac{1}{2m} \nabla_{\mathbf{\theta}} \|\mathbf{y}_i - \mathbf{\hat{y}}_i\|^2 \\
&= \frac{1}{2m} \nabla_{\mathbf{\theta}} \|\mathbf{y}_i - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\|^2 \\
&= \frac{1}{2m} \nabla_{\mathbf{\theta}} ((\mathbf{y}_i - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta})^T (\mathbf{y}_i - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta})) \\
&= \frac{1}{2m} \nabla_{\mathbf{\theta}} ((\mathbf{y}_i^T - \boldsymbol{\theta}^T \mathbf{X}^T) (\mathbf{y}_i - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta})) \\
&= \frac{1}{2m} \nabla_{\mathbf{\theta}} (\mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta} - \boldsymbol{\theta}^T \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} + \boldsymbol{\theta}^T \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}) \\
&= \frac{1}{2m} \nabla_{\mathbf{\theta}} (-2\boldsymbol{\theta}^T \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} + \boldsymbol{\theta}^T \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}) \\
&= \frac{1}{2m} (-2\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} + 2\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}) \\
&= \frac{1}{m} (-\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} + \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}) \\
\Rightarrow \boldsymbol{\theta} &= (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}
\end{aligned}
\]
We found the solution for the best \(\theta\)s that minimize our error function. Notice that the matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) should contain a column of ones as its first column for the bias term in the \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) vector. So why do we need a gradient descent algorithm if we can find the solution directly? There are several reasons. First, the matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) can be very large, so the multiplication and the inversion can be very expensive to compute and require a lot of memory. Second, the equation above is only true for the MSE loss function and does not apply to a general loss function.
Instead of using the direct approach, we can use the gradient descent algorithm, which is an iterative algorithm. The main idea behind the gradient descent is to look at the direction of the steepest descent at our current position on the error function and make a small step in this direction. Recall we look at the loss function in the parameters space and look for the minimum of it. If we move in the direction of the descent, we hope to find, eventually, the parameters that minimize it.
At each iteration, we compute the gradient of the loss function and update the parameters by moving a little step in the negative direction of the gradient of the loss (this is the steepest descent).
\[
\boldsymbol{\theta} := \boldsymbol{\theta} - \alpha \nabla_{\mathbf{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
\]
The hyper-parameter α is calling the learning rate, and it determines the step size we take in the descent direction. We keep updating the parameters until convergence of the loss function (or for some predefined number of iterations). Pay attention that if the loss function is not convex, we may end in a local minimum instead of the optimal global minimum.

title: Linear Regression with Gradient Descent from Scratch
text:
Time to Code
Let’s write a class that performs a linear regression. We start by writing the whole code, and then we will explain each step.
import numpy as np

class LinearRegression:
    def __init__(self, learning_rate=0.01, max_num_iteration=10000, eps=1e-6):
        self.learning_rate = learning_rate
        self.max_num_iteration = max_num_iteration
        self.eps = eps
        self.bias = 0
        self.weights = None

    def fit(self, X, y):
        num_sample, num_features = X.shape
        self.weights = np.zeros(num_features)
        weights_and_bias = np.zeros(num_features + 1)
        X_with_bias = np.hstack((np.ones((num_sample, 1)), X))

        for _ in range(self.max_num_iteration):
            y_predicted = self.predict(X)

            d_loss = 1 / num_sample * X_with_bias.T @ (y_predicted - y)

            weights_and_bias -= self.learning_rate * d_loss
            self.bias = weights_and_bias[0]
            self.weights =  weights_and_bias[1:].copy()

            if np.max(np.abs(y_predicted - self.predict(X))) < self.eps:
                break

    def predict(self, X):
        return X @ self.weights + self.bias
First, we define a LinearRegression class and initialize it with the learning rate, the maximum number of iterations, and some epsilon value to determine convergence. We also initialize the bias term to 0 and set the weights to None since we don’t know yet how many features we have.
In the fit method, we try to find the bias and the weights using gradient descent. As we saw earlier, the gradient of the loss is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_{\mathbf{\theta}}\mathcal{L} &= \frac{1}{m}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta} - \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}) \\
&= \frac{1}{m}\mathbf{X}^T(\mathbf{\hat{y}} - \mathbf{y})
\end{aligned}
\]
So, we first construct the \(\mathbf{X}\) matrix to include an additional column with ones for the bias term, and we create a vector of zeros for the bias term and the weights. Then, in each iteration, we find the prediction \(\hat{y}\), compute the derivate of the loss, and update the bias and the weights. Finally, we check if the new prediction changed enough relative to the old prediction to determine if we converge.
The predict method uses the bias and weights we found for the model to predict the result from the data.
Let’s try it.
theta_1 = 2
theta_0 = 1
X = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)[:, None]
y = np.squeeze(theta_1 * X + theta_0) + np.random.normal(scale=1, size=X.shape[0])
lin = LinearRegression()
lin.fit(X, y)
We create a synthetic dataset of a simple line of the form \(y = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x\), and we also add some noise to \(y\). Then, we try to find the line from the data with our class. The results are as follows.



Linear regression model fit result plot


The blue dots are the data we fitted for, and the orange line is the model found. The bias term is 1.03, and the weight is 1.99, which shows a very good fitting.

title: Paper Review: Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL)
text:
In a previous post, we talked about the importance of self-supervised learning and why we would like to use it. Let’s repeat the main points. As we know, deep learning models need an extensive labeled dataset to learn from. While in a lot of cases, collecting the data itself is not a too hard task, the labeling step could be very time and money consuming, but this step is crucial for the classic supervised learning methods.
Self-supervised techniques can solve this problem by letting models learn from unlabeled data. It does so by learning meaningful representations directly from the data, without any need for labels.
In the previous post, we focused on the SimCLR architecture based on the contrastive learning method, which uses positive and negative sample pairs to teach models distinguishing features, by mapping similar samples (positives) closer together in the feature space while pushing dissimilar samples (negatives) farther apart. However, this method comes with significant computational costs and practical challenges. “Bootstrap Your Own Latent” (BYOL) brings a new approach to the field by proposing a way to learn without the need for negative pairs, making it both efficient and highly scalable.
In this post, we’ll explore how BYOL works, the problem it solves, its architectural design, and why it’s considered a breakthrough in self-supervised learning.

title: Paper Review: Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL)
section: The Problem: Dependency on Negative Samples
text:
The Problem: Dependency on Negative Samples
As mentioned above, contrastive learning tries to find representations that keep pairs of positive examples (which are two augmented views of the same image) close, while negative samples (views from different images) representations are pushed farther apart. In this way, the model can learn distinct representations.
However, this method has limitations:

Risk of representation collapse: Without enough negative examples, contrastive learning methods can sometimes yield trivial representations that fail to capture useful features.
High computational costs: Contrastive learning often requires large batch sizes to provide diverse negative samples, leading to increased memory and computational requirements.
Batch size dependency: The method’s success often hinges on having a substantial number of negative samples, which becomes a problem when the batch size is small.

As the last two points are a result of the first one, let’s expand a bit on the first point. Because we ask our model to find representations such that two views of the same image have similar representations, the model may come up with a constant representation for all images. Such a representation fulfills this goal, but it is not much of a help. By adding negative samples (i.e., other images), we add to the original task another task of discrimination between the representations of different images. This addition is the key to preventing collapsed representations.
It is found empirically that the number of negative samples and their quality have a strong influence on the result of this technique. This is the reason why it needs a large batch size and has high computational costs.
BYOL proposes a novel approach that eliminates the need for negative samples. Instead, it leverages two networks — a target network and an online network — that interact with different augmented views of the same image to refine each other’s representations iteratively. BYOL avoids collapse and complex negative sampling strategies and presents an efficient and stable learning solution that we will talk about next.

title: Paper Review: Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL)
text:
BYOL’s Core Idea
A simple solution to prevent collapse is to use a fixed randomly initialized network to produce the target representation of the predictions our main network produces. The authors found empirically that although it does avoid collapse, the result representations are not very good, but still much better than the initial fixed representation.
This experimental finding is the main idea behind BYOL. We start with a target representation, and we train a new and potentially enhanced representation, referred to as online, by predicting the target representation. Later we can use the updated online representation as the new target and iteratively repeat the procedure. In practice, the authors suggest using a slowly moving exponential average of the online network as the target network, instead of fixed checkpoints.

title: Paper Review: Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL)
text:
BYOL’s Architecture: How It Works
BYOL’s approach is to create two augmented views of an image — two different transformations of the same input — and pass them through separate networks, “online” and “target”, where the online network tries to predict the target output.



BYOL’s architecture. BYOL minimizes a similarity loss between \(q_\theta(z_\theta)\) and \(\text{sg}(z'_\xi)\), where \(\theta\) are the trained weights, \(\xi\) are an exponential moving average of \(\theta\) and \(\text{sg}\) means stop-gradient. At the end of training, everything but \(f_\theta\) is discarded, and \(y_\theta\) is used as the image representation. Source:  Bootstrap Your Own Latent A New Approach to Self-Supervised Learning 


Let’s break down the architecture:

Online Network
The online network processes one view of the image and consists of three key stages:

Encoder \(f_\theta\): This is the primary network, often a convolutional neural network (CNN) like ResNet, that processes the image and extracts features. The encoder produces high-dimensional embeddings that capture the main features.
Projector \(g_\theta\): Following the encoder there is a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) projector. This projector transforms the high-dimensional representation into a lower-dimensional latent space.
Predictor \(q_\theta\): Exclusive to the online network, the predictor maps the projected feature representation to align with the target network’s output. This component helps the online network to closely match the target’s output.



Target Network
The target network mirrors the online network’s structure, containing an encoder and a projector. However, it lacks a predictor. The target network serves as a stable reference point for the online network to align with, and its weights are updated gradually using an exponential moving average (EMA) of the online network’s weights. This EMA process is crucial for maintaining stability, preventing the model from collapsing to trivial solutions.


The Loss Function
BYOL employs a simple mean squared error between the normalized prediction and target projections, which can be shown to be a sort of cosine similarity loss.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}_{\theta,\xi} &= \|\overline{q_\theta}(z_\theta) - \overline{z}'_\xi\|_2^2 \\
&= \left\| \frac{q_\theta(z_\theta)}{\|q_\theta(z_\theta)\|_2} - \frac{z'_\xi}{\|z'_\xi\|_2} \right\|_2^2 \\
&= \sum_i \left( \frac{q_{\theta_i}(z_\theta)}{\|q_\theta(z_\theta)\|_2} - \frac{z'_{\xi_i}}{\|z'_\xi\|_2} \right)^2 \\
&= \sum_i \left( \frac{q_{\theta_i}^2(z_\theta)}{\|q_\theta(z_\theta)\|_2^2} + \frac{z'^2_{\xi_i}}{\|z'_\xi\|_2^2} - 2\frac{q_{\theta_i}(z_\theta) \cdot z'_{\xi_i}}{\|q_\theta(z_\theta)\|_2 \cdot \|z'_\xi\|_2} \right) \\
&= \sum_i \frac{q_{\theta_i}^2(z_\theta)}{\|q_\theta(z_\theta)\|_2^2} + \sum_i \frac{z'^2_{\xi_i}}{\|z'_\xi\|_2^2} - 2\sum_i \frac{q_{\theta_i}(z_\theta) \cdot z'_{\xi_i}}{\|q_\theta(z_\theta)\|_2 \cdot \|z'_\xi\|_2} \\
&= 1 + 1 - 2\frac{\langle q_\theta(z_\theta), z'_\xi \rangle}{\|q_\theta(z_\theta)\|_2 \cdot \|z'_\xi\|_2} \\
&= 2 - 2\frac{\langle q_\theta(z_\theta), z'_\xi \rangle}{\|q_\theta(z_\theta)\|_2 \cdot \|z'_\xi\|_2}
\end{aligned}
\]
The goal is to minimize the difference between these two representations, encouraging the online network to match the target’s stable reference. Unlike contrastive methods that require both positive and negative samples, BYOL’s loss is based solely on positive alignment, eliminating the need for direct contrast.
At each step, this loss is computed twice, wherein the second time we switch between the two augmented views so each of them will be passed to the other network. The final loss is the addition of the two losses.


Exponential Moving Average (EMA) Update
A pivotal part of BYOL is the slow, smoothing update of the target network’s weights using EMA. In each training step, the target network’s weights become a mix of its current weights and those of the online network. This creates a progressively refined target, which helps prevent representation collapse and allows the network to focus on meaningful features over time.
More formally, at each step, we compute the two losses, add them, make the optimization step to update the online network weights, and finally update the target weights as follows.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}_{\theta,\xi}^{\text{BYOL}} &= \mathcal{L}_{\theta,\xi} + \tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\theta,\xi} \\
\theta &\leftarrow \text{optimizer}(\theta, \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\theta,\xi}^{\text{BYOL}}, \eta) \\
\xi &\leftarrow \tau\xi + (1 - \tau)\theta
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\tau\) is the decay rate of the EMA and \(\eta\) is the learning rate.

title: Paper Review: Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL)
text:
Main Code Implementation
In this section, we will write the main components of BYOL architecture. Although this is not a full implementation, it still should give you an understanding of how to implement it.
Let’s import some necessary modules.
from copy import deepcopy

import torch
from torch import nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torchvision import models
We start with the components of the online network. For the encoder, we can use ResNet50, for example. ResNet50 can be downloaded directly from torchvision.
backbone = models.resnet50(weights=None)
backbone_without_classifier = nn.Sequential(*list(backbone.children())[:-1])
online_encoder = backbone_without_classifier
In the code, we got the ResNet50 architecture with random initialization. The original ResNet is built to predict ImageNet classes, so we remove the classifier component from it since we only want the features extracted from it.
We continue to the online projection which is a simple MLP.
online_projection = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Flatten(),
            nn.Linear(backbone.fc.in_features, 4096),
            nn.BatchNorm1d(4096),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Linear(4096, 256)
        )
And the predictor is the same.
online_prediction = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(256, 4096),
            nn.BatchNorm1d(4096),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Linear(4096, 256)
        )
For the target network, we clone the online network’s encoder and projector.
target_encoder = deepcopy(online_encoder)
target_projection = deepcopy(online_projection)
and since we don’t need gradients for the target network, we can set all its parameters to not track gradients.
for param in target_encoder.parameters():
    param.requires_grad = False

for param in target_projection.parameters():
    param.requires_grad = False
We define the loss as a module (you can also define it as a regular function)
class BYOLLoss(nn.Module):
    """
    Loss function for self supervised learning based on
    the paper "Bootstrap Your Own Latent A New Approach
    to Self-Supervised Learning" equation (2).
    """
    @staticmethod
    def forward(prediction, projection):
        """

        Args:
            prediction (torch.Tensor): the instance representation prediction
                of the online network.
            projection (torch.Tensor): the instance representation of the
                target network.

        Returns:

        """
        loss = 2 - 2 * F.cosine_similarity(prediction, projection)
        return loss.mean()
and finally, a function to update the target network’s weights with an exponential moving average.
def update_target_models(online, target, moving_average_decay):
    """
    Update the weights of the target models (encoder and projection)
    using exponential moving average with the online models. For more 
    information about the technique, refer to the paper "Bootstrap Your 
    Own Latent A New Approach to Self-Supervised Learning"

    Args:
      online (nn.Module): a component of the online network
      target (nn.Module): a component of the target network, 
        the same as the online one
      moving_average_decay (float): the decay rate of the exponential 
        moving average. Number between 0 and 1.
    """
    for online_params, target_params in zip(online.parameters(), target.parameters()):
        target_params.data = (target_params.data * moving_average_decay
                              + (1 - moving_average_decay) * online_params.data)
These are the main components we need to implement BYOL. For the training itself, you need to create a dataset that returns two augmented views of the image (you can read about the specific augmentations in the paper). Then, first pass the first view to the online network, and the second to the target network and compute the loss. After that, pass the second view to the online network and the first one to the target network, and compute the loss. Use the combined loss to update the online network’s weights, and then update the target network’s weights using the exponential moving average.

Conclusion
BYOL brings several significant benefits to self-supervised learning, thanks to its architecture and loss design. BYOL’s approach gives us several advantages:

Avoidance of Negative Samples
By eliminating the need for negative pairs, BYOL bypasses the high resource demands of contrastive learning. It’s a considerable advantage in applications with limited computational resources, as it reduces the dependence on large batch sizes and complicated negative sample strategies. BYOL’s innovative design shows that useful features can be learned solely through positive reinforcement, making it a more efficient solution.
Reduced Risk of Representation Collapse
Representation collapse — where a network produces the same outputs regardless of the input — can be a common problem in self-supervised models. BYOL’s use of a predictor in the online network, combined with EMA-updated target weights, allows it to avoid collapse, making it more stable and robust.
Simplicity and Scalability
BYOL’s architecture is simple and highly scalable, requiring fewer hyperparameters than contrastive methods. This simplicity enables it to be easily adapted to various architectures.

BYOL has a great impact on the field of self-supervised learning by showing that meaningful representations can be learned without negative samples. The success of BYOL shows the potential of innovative self-supervised learning methods and lays the foundations for future advancements in resource-efficient models.
By demonstrating that robust features can be learned without complex contrastive methods, BYOL is used as a base for new research directions. If you work on a task with a big dataset, but limited labels, BYOL offers you a highly effective solution to increase your system performance.

title: Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 7
text:
This post is part of a series of posts about diffusion models:

Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 1
Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 2
Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 3
Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 4
Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 5
Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 6
Intro to Diffusion Model — Part 7 (this post)
Full implementation

Before we train, we need a dataset. I chose to work here with the Smithsonian butterflies dataset from Hugging Face. First, we need to install the Hugging Face dataset module.
pip install datasets[vision] -q
Then, we can load the Smithsonian butterflies dataset.
from datasets import load_dataset
dataset = load_dataset("huggan/smithsonian_butterflies_subset", split='train')
Now, we want to create a data loader with this dataset and apply transformation in a similar way to what we did in part 4.
from torchvision.transforms import RandomHorizontalFlip, Compose, ToTensor, Resize, Normalize
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

image_size = 64
transform = Compose([
  Resize((image_size, image_size)),
  RandomHorizontalFlip(),
  ToTensor(),
  Normalize(mean=(0.5, 0.5, 0.5), std=(0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
])

def transforms(data):
  images = [transform(im) for im in data['image']]
  return {'images': images}

dataset.set_transform(transforms)

batch_size=32
train_dataloader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True)
We can look at an example from the dataset with
batch = next(iter(train_dataloader))
reverse_transform_pil(batch['images'][20])



An example of a butterfly image from the Smithsonian butterflies dataset after applying transformations


We need to define a loss for the training. Here, we are going to use L1.
import torch.nn.functional as F

def compute_loss(model, x0, t, noise=None):
  if noise is None:
    noise = torch.randn_like(x0)

  x_t = sample_q(x0, t, noise)
  predicted_noise = model(x_t, t)
  loss = F.l1_loss(noise, predicted_noise)
  return loss
Now, we can initialize the model and set an optimizer.
from torch.optim import Adam

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
model = DiffusionUnet(dim=image_size, channels=3, dim_mults=(1, 2, 4, 8)).to(device)
optimizer = Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-4)
We will want to save results along the training, so we create a results folder.
from pathlib import Path
results_folder = Path("./results")
results_folder.mkdir(exist_ok = True)
For the training, I’m going to use Google Colab, so I want to save the model to my Google Drive and continue the training later in case of a timeout. For that, we need to connect to Google Drive first.
from google.colab import drive
drive.mount('/content/gdrive')
Now, we check if we already have a model saved in our drive. If there is, we load it; otherwise, we create an empty dictionary.
model_saved_file_path = Path('/content/gdrive/MyDrive/diffusion_checkpoints/saved_model.pth')
if model_saved_file_path.exists():
  saved_model = torch.load(str(model_saved_file_path))
else:
  model_saved_file_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
  saved_model = {}
  start_epoch = 0

if saved_model:
    print('loading model')
    model.load_state_dict(saved_model['model'])
    optimizer.load_state_dict(saved_model['optimizer'])
    current_epoch = saved_model['epoch']
And finally, we implement the training loop.
import numpy as np
from torchvision.utils import save_image
epochs = 1000
loss_steps = 50
sample_every = 1000
loss_for_mean = np.zeros(loss_steps)
prev_time = time.time()

for epoch in range(start_epoch, epochs):
  for batch_index, batch in enumerate(train_dataloader):
    images = batch['images'].to(device)
    # sample t according to Algorithm 1
    t = torch.randint(1, num_timesteps, (images.shape[0],), device=device).long()
    loss = compute_loss(model, images, t)
    current_step = batch_index + epoch * len(train_dataloader)
    if current_step % loss_steps == 0:

      # Determine approximate time left
      batches_done = epoch * len(train_dataloader) + batch_index
      batches_left = epochs * len(train_dataloader) - current_step
      time_left = datetime.timedelta(seconds=batches_left * (time.time() - prev_time) / loss_steps)
      prev_time = time.time()

      print(f'Loss at epoch {epoch}, batch {batch_index}: {loss_for_mean.mean()} | time remaining: {time_left}')
      loss_for_mean[:] = 0
    loss_for_mean[current_step%loss_steps] = loss.item()

    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

    if current_step % sample_every == 0:
      batch_to_sample = 5
      sample_images_list = sampling(model, (batch_to_sample, 3, image_size, image_size))
      sample_images = torch.cat(sample_images_list, dim=0)
      sample_images = reverse_transform_tensor(sample_images)
      save_image(sample_images, str(results_folder / f'sample_{current_step}.png'), nrow=batch_to_sample)

  saved_model['epoch'] = epoch + 1
  saved_model['model'] = model.state_dict()
  saved_model['optimizer']= optimizer.state_dict()
  torch.save(saved_model, '/content/gdrive/MyDrive/diffusion_checkpoints/saved_model.pth')
We train according to Algorithm 1 from part 3. We get a batch of clean images and sample the timestamp uniformly, and then we try to predict the noise we have added to the images and compute the loss. We save the loss values for loss_steps steps (a step is one batch from the data loader), and after that, we print the mean of the loss over the last loss_steps steps. Pay attention that the loss printed the first time is meaningless since the loss_for_mean buffer is not full yet. We also estimate the time remaining and print it with the loss. We update the weights of the model, and once every sample_every steps we sample from the reverse process and save the result. Finally, at the end of each epoch, we save the states of the model and the optimizer together with the current epoch index.
After finishing the training, we can sample new butterfly images with the following code:
from torchvision.utils import make_grid
reverse_transform_pil(make_grid(sampling(model, (16, 3, 64, 64))[-1], nrow=8))



Samples of butterflies after 1000 epochs


We can also see the reverse process using
from torchvision.utils import make_grid
image_steps_list = sampling(model, (4, 3, 64, 64), 300)
image_steps = torch.cat(image_steps_list, dim=0)
reverse_transform_pil(make_grid(image_steps, nrow=4))
The code above will show the last 300 steps of sampling 4 butterflies.

title: Harris Corners Detector — from Theory to Code
text:
In many computer vision tasks, we need to find some interest points — points in the image we can detect and describe and then use for a task, such as image-stitching and detection.
The first question one should ask is what is a good interest point (also called a feature). We want such a point to be well-defined so we can detect it precisely and repetitively. To get a feeling of what is a good feature point, let’s look at some scenarios in an image. First, we look at a point with similar values around it, like a middle of a black square.
This is not a good feature since we can’t detect it precisely. We can move the red square a little in any direction, and we don’t even know we have moved.
Now, let’s look at an edge:
If the red square moves a little to the right or to the left, we can see something has changed, but if it moves a little up or down, we can’t tell if something has changed. So this is also not a good feature to detect precisely.
What about the corner?
Here any movement of the red square results in some changes inside it. We can say exactly where this point is! Think about it, if I ask you to point to the center of the square, you can only guess where it is and pick some point in the area of the center. But, if I ask you to point to the top left corner, you know exactly where it is. Thus, the corner is a good feature.
What characterizes the corner is that it has gradients (changes) in more than one direction, so it is easy to say if something changes when we move a little.

title: Harris Corners Detector — from Theory to Code
text:
The Mathematics
We want now to formulate the idea of changes when moving a little bit from a pixel in the image. For that, we introduce the following error function:
\[
E(u, v) = \sum_{x,y} w(x,y) \left[ I(x+u, y+v) - I(x,y) \right]^2
\]
where \(x\) and \(y\) are the pixel’s coordinates, \(u\) and \(v\) are a shift amount, \(I\) is the intensity of the image at some point (the value of a pixel), and \(w\) is a window function. This formula calculates the error we will get if we move the image by \(u\) and \(v\) (inside some window).



An image I with a window (left) and the error as a function of the shift (right)


In the figure above, you can see that at \(E(0, 0)\) (the center), the value is 0 (perfect black) since there are no changes with a shift of zero, and so the error function got zero. When the shift becomes bigger, the error function gets bigger too.
A corner region should change even for a small shift, so we want to see what happens to the error function for a small shift. For that, we can use the Taylor series. We are going to develop a second-order expansion of the error function, but first, let’s recall how a second-order Taylor series around \(x_0\) looks like
\[
f(x - x_0) \approx f(x_0) + f'(x_0)(x - x_0) + \frac{1}{2} f''(x_0)(x - x_0)^2
\]
for the error function expansion, we set \(x_0 = 0\), so
\[
f(x) \approx f(0) + f'(0)x + \frac{1}{2} f''(0)x^2
\]
but the error function is a two-variable function, so the Taylor series is a little more complicated and can be written in a matrix notation as
\[
E(u, v) \approx E(0,0) + \begin{bmatrix} u & v \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} E_u(0,0) \\ E_v(0,0) \end{bmatrix} + \frac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} u & v \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} E_{uu}(0,0) & E_{uv}(0,0) \\ E_{uv}(0,0) & E_{vv}(0,0) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}
\]
where the \(u\) and \(v\) subscript mean derivative according to \(u\) and \(v\), respectively (and \(uu\) is the second derivative according to \(u\) and so on). You can expand the expression above and see this is a regular 2-dimensional Taylor series.
Let’s calculate the first derivatives:
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_u(u,v) &= \sum_{x,y} 2w(x,y) \left[ I(x+u,y+v) - I(x,y) \right] I_x(x+u,y+v) \\
E_v(u,v) &= \sum_{x,y} 2w(x,y) \left[ I(x+u,y+v) - I(x,y) \right] I_y(x+u,y+v)
\end{aligned}
\]
Notice that the direction of \(u\) is the same as \(x\), and the direction of \(v\) is the same as \(y\). For the second derivatives:
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_{uu}(u,v) &= \sum_{x,y} 2w(x,y) I_x(x+u,y+v) I_x(x+u,y+v) \\
&\quad + \sum_{x,y} 2w(x,y) \left[ I(x+u,y+v) - I(x,y) \right] I_{xx}(x+u,y+v)
\end{aligned}
\]
and similarly for \(v\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_{vv}(u,v) &= \sum_{x,y} 2w(x,y) I_y(x+u,y+v) I_y(x+u,y+v) \\
&\quad + \sum_{x,y} 2w(x,y) \left[ I(x+u,y+v) - I(x,y) \right] I_{yy}(x+u,y+v)
\end{aligned}
\]
and the cross derivative
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_{uv}(u,v) &= \sum_{x,y} 2w(x,y) I_y(x+u,y+v) I_x(x+u,y+v) \\
&\quad + \sum_{x,y} 2w(x,y) \left[ I(x+u,y+v) - I(x,y) \right] I_{xy}(x+u,y+v)
\end{aligned}
\]
Recall now that we evaluate the derivative at \((u, v) = (0, 0)\), so a lot of things are going to vanish.
\[
\begin{aligned}
E(0,0) &= 0 \\
E_u(0,0) &= 0 \\
E_v(0,0) &= 0 \\
E_{uu}(0,0) &= \sum_{x,y} 2w(x,y) I_x(x,y) I_x(x,y) \\
E_{vv}(0,0) &= \sum_{x,y} 2w(x,y) I_y(x,y) I_y(x,y) \\
E_{uv}(0,0) &= \sum_{x,y} 2w(x,y) I_y(x,y) I_x(x,y)
\end{aligned}
\]
Notice there are no more second or cross derivatives of \(I\). Now we can rewrite the equation for the error function as
\[
E(u, v) \approx \begin{bmatrix} u & v \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \sum_{x,y} w(x,y) I_x^2(x,y) & \sum_{x,y} w(x,y) I_x(x,y) I_y(x,y) \\ \sum_{x,y} w(x,y) I_x(x,y) I_y(x,y) & \sum_{x,y} w(x,y) I_y^2(x,y) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}
\]
The matrix in the equation above can be written as
\[
M = \sum_{x,y} w(x,y) \begin{bmatrix} I_x^2 & I_x I_y \\ I_x I_y & I_y^2 \end{bmatrix}
\]
Now, let’s suppose we can write the matrix \(M\) using the eigen decomposition so
\[
M = P \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1 & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_2 \end{bmatrix} P^{-1}
\]
where \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are the eigenvalues of \(M\) and \(P\) is a matrix with eigenvectors as columns
\[
P = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v}_1 & \mathbf{v}_2 \end{bmatrix}
\]
We can write the vector \(\mathbf{u} = [u, v]\) using a linear combination of the eigenvectors as
\[
\mathbf{u} = a \mathbf{v}_1 + b \mathbf{v}_2
\]
and recall that if \(\mathbf{v}_1\) is an eigenvector of the matrix \(M\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\), then
\[
M \mathbf{v}_1 = \lambda_1 \mathbf{v}_1
\]
Let’s use all of that in the function of the error.
\[
\begin{aligned}
E(u,v) &= \mathbf{u}^T M \mathbf{u} = (a \mathbf{v}_1 + b \mathbf{v}_2)^T M (a \mathbf{v}_1 + b \mathbf{v}_2) \\
&= (a \mathbf{v}_1^T + b \mathbf{v}_2^T)(a \lambda_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + b \lambda_2 \mathbf{v}_2) \\
&= \lambda_1 a^2 + \lambda_2 b^2 \\
&= \frac{a^2}{\left(\lambda_1^{-1/2}\right)^2} + \frac{b^2}{\left(\lambda_2^{-1/2}\right)^2}
\end{aligned}
\]
We assume the eigenvectors are normalized, and also they are orthogonal (so their dot product is 0). Notice that the last expression is an expression of an ellipse for some constant error. The ellipse axes are according to the direction of the eigenvectors, and their length is according to the eigenvalues. The values of \(a\) and \(b\) are the length in the direction of \(\mathbf{v}_1\) and \(\mathbf{v}_2\) that are needed to reconstruct the vector \(\mathbf{u}\).



The question that arises now is what is the meaning of the result above. Let’s start by assuming both \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are small numbers. In this case, the axes of the ellipse will be very large. That means we need a big step in any of the eigenvector directions to get a high error, which means that the image is relatively flat (slow changes).
If, on the other hand, \(\lambda_1 \gg \lambda_2\), the axis in \(\mathbf{v}_1\) direction will be much smaller than the one of \(\mathbf{v}_2\). If so, for some error, a little step in \(\mathbf{v}_1\) direction will be sufficient to satisfy the equation, but if we choose to go with the other direction, we need a much bigger step. This is a case of an edge in the image, where one direction causes a little change and so a little error, while the other direction can make a big change with a small shift.
Finally, if \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both large and similar in size, the ellipse will be small and with a shape more similar to a circle which implies a significant change in all directions. This is a case of a corner.



The calculation of the eigenvalues can be expensive, but since we are interested in the relation between the eigenvalues, we don’t actually need to compute them. Instead, recall that the determinant of a matrix is the multiplication of the eigenvalues, and the trace (sum of the elements on the diagonal) is the sum of the eigenvalues. So, instead of getting the eigenvalues themselves, we can calculate another number — \(R.\)
\[
R = \text{det}(M) - \alpha \text{trace}(M)^2 = \lambda_1 \lambda_2 - \alpha (\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)^2
\]
where \(\alpha\) is a constant between 0.04 and 0.06 found empirically. If both eigenvalues are large, the value of \(R\) will be large, and it’s a corner. If just one of the eigenvalues is large, the result of \(R\) will be a large negative value. And, if the magnitude of \(R\) is small, this is the case of a “flat” region where the eigenvalues are small numbers.

title: Harris Corners Detector — from Theory to Code
text:
Harris Corners Detector Algorithm
The algorithm for detecting corners is as follows:

Convert the image into a gray-scale image
Apply Gaussian blurring to reduce noise
Take derivatives in both \(x\) and \(y\) directions for each pixel
Compute the \(M\) matrix using a window around each pixel
Compute \(R\)
Threshold \(R\)
For accurate localization, one can add non-maximum suppression

title: Harris Corners Detector — from Theory to Code
text:
Coding It
Let’s write a simple code to find corners and mark them with red circles. First, we import the necessary modules
import numpy as np
from numpy.linalg import det
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import cv2  # OpenCV
We define a function for non-maximum suppression
def non_maximum_suppression(matrix, kernel_size=5):
    kernel = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_RECT, (kernel_size, kernel_size))  # rectangular kernel
    maxed_matrix  = cv2.dilate(matrix, kernel)  # get maximum value in the window for each pixel
    non_maximum_suppression_matrix = matrix.copy()
    non_maximum_suppression_matrix[matrix != maxed_matrix] = 0  # set to 0 pixel originally are not local maxima
    return non_maximum_suppression_matrix
And implement a function for the Harris detector algorithm
def corner_detector(image, window_size, k, threshold):
    image_copy = image.copy()  # get copy of the image so the original one won't be changed
    height = image.shape[0]
    width = image.shape[1]
    # step 1: convert to gray-scale
    gray_image = cv2.cvtColor(image, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    # step 2: reduce noise using Gaussian blurring
    image_blurred = cv2.GaussianBlur(gray_image, (3, 3), 0)
    
    # step 3: get the derivatives using Sobel operator
    Ix = cv2.Sobel(image_blurred, cv2.CV_64F, 1, 0, ksize=3)
    Iy = cv2.Sobel(image_blurred, cv2.CV_64F, 0, 1, ksize=3)
    # compute the basic components of the M matrix
    IxIx = Ix ** 2
    IyIy = Iy ** 2
    IxIy = Ix * Iy

    offset = window_size // 2  # offset from the edge of the image so the all window will be inside the image
    image_R_matrix = np.zeros((height, width))
    # go over each pixel
    for y in range(offset, height - offset):
        for x in range(offset, width - offset):
            #  step 4: compute the element of the M matrix
            M_00 = np.sum(IxIx[y-offset:y+offset+1, x-offset:x+offset+1])
            M_11 = np.sum(IyIy[y-offset:y+offset+1, x-offset:x+offset+1])
            M_01 = np.sum(IxIy[y-offset:y+offset+1, x-offset:x+offset+1])
            M = np.array([[M_00, M_01], [M_01, M_11]])
            #  step 5: compute R
            R = det(M) - k * (np.trace(M) ** 2)
            image_R_matrix[y, x] = R

    # normalize the values of Rs to be between 0 and 1
    cv2.normalize(image_R_matrix, image_R_matrix, alpha=0, beta=1, norm_type=cv2.NORM_MINMAX)
    #  step 6: thresholding R
    is_corner = image_R_matrix > threshold
    image_R_matrix[~is_corner] = 0
    #  step 7: apply non-maximum suppression
    image_R_matrix = non_maximum_suppression(image_R_matrix)
    
    #  draw circle around the corners
    for y in range(offset, height - offset):
        for x in range(offset, width - offset):
            if image_R_matrix[y, x] != 0:
                cv2.circle(image_copy, (x, y), 1, (0, 0, 255), -1)

    return image_copy
And we can use the code with
image = cv2.imread('./im.jpg')
corner_image = corner_detector(image, 5, 0.04, 0.24)
plt.imshow(corner_image[:, :, ::-1])
plt.show()
and the final result:

title: CLIP — Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training
text:
In the world of modern AI, computer vision has long been treated as a solitary field. For years, the standard approach to understanding images was to analyze them in a vacuum — either by classifying pixels into rigid, predefined categories or trying to reconstruct them using architectures like Autoencoders and VAEs. But the human experience isn’t unimodal; we don’t just look at the world, we can also describe it.
This is where Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) changes the game. By bridging the gap between vision and language, CLIP changes the traditional analysis of images and explores a powerful approach: multimodal learning. Instead of training a model to analyze images in isolation, CLIP learns to connect the dots between two entirely different worlds — images and the natural language captions that describe them. By training on massive amounts of paired data, its mission is to take any arbitrary, never-before-seen image-text pair and accurately measure how well they align. The secret to unlocking this flexible, cross-modal understanding? It all comes down to a brilliantly designed loss function.

title: CLIP — Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training
section: The Core Intuition: What is Contrastive Learning?
text:
The Core Intuition: What is Contrastive Learning?
Contrastive learning is a technique where a model learns to distinguish between similar and dissimilar data points. The core idea is to map similar samples (positives) closer together in the feature space while pushing dissimilar samples (negatives) farther apart. There are many cases where contrastive learning and contrastive loss can be used. For example, it is used extensively across self-supervised learning, with prominent examples including methods like SimCLR or BYOL.
In CLIP, the main goal is to map an image directly to its descriptive text. For each batch of data, the model aims to produce similar representations for an image and its associated caption, while keeping that representation distant from the captions of all other images in the batch.
Through this approach, the model learns to connect visual information with textual information. By operating across two distinct modalities at once, CLIP achieved a major milestone in representation learning.



Similar images and captions should be close together, while different concepts should be kept apart

title: CLIP — Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training
section: The Architecture: Two Encoders, One Shared Space
text:
The Architecture: Two Encoders, One Shared Space
Images and text belong to two distinct modalities — meaning they are fundamentally different information structures. If our goal is to relate an image to a text caption, we must first bring them into a shared space where they can be directly compared and measured for similarity.
To accomplish this, CLIP uses two dedicated encoders to extract feature representations from each domain: a ResNet or Vision Transformer (ViT) for images, and a standard Transformer for text. Ultimately, these two encoders map both distinct data types into fixed-size feature vectors within the exact same embedding dimension, enabling direct mathematical comparison.



Images and text pairs are processed by two types of encoders to produce a single vector representation that can be compared. Source:  Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision

title: CLIP — Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training
text:
Multi-Modal Contrastive Loss
Once we have these vector representations, the next step is determining how to compare them and how to use that comparison for training. The central intuition is straightforward: for a true (image, text) pair, the two feature vectors should be highly similar, whereas vectors from unmatched pairs should be distinct.
A standard way to measure similarity between two vectors is cosine similarity, which is the normalized dot product of the vectors.
Given a batch of \(N\) (image, text) pairs, the encoders produce \(N\) image embedding vectors and \(N\) text embedding vectors. Pairwise evaluation yields an \(N \times N\) similarity matrix containing \(N^2\) similarity scores. The \(N\) diagonal entries correspond to the true matching (image, text) pairs and should have high similarity scores, while the remaining \(N^2 - N\) off-diagonal entries represent unmatched pairs and should have low scores.
To maximize diagonal scores while minimizing off-diagonal scores, CLIP uses a symmetric cross-entropy loss. This involves computing standard cross-entropy loss on the similarity matrix in both directions and averaging the two terms:
Image-to-Text Loss (\(\mathcal{L}_I\)): For each image, predict which of the \(N\) text captions matches it (Given Image \(i\), how well can the model pick out Text \(i\) from all \(N\) texts?). For each row \(i\), a Softmax function is applied across the columns to turn raw similarity scores into a probability distribution over the text captions. Categorical cross-entropy is then calculated against the ground-truth diagonal index:
\[
\mathcal{L}_I = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log \frac{\exp(S_{i,i})}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} \exp(S_{i,j})}
\]
Text-to-Image Loss (\(\mathcal{L}_T\)): For each text caption, predict which of the \(N\) images matches it. (Given Text \(j\), how well can the model pick out Image \(j\) from all \(N\) images?). For each column \(j\), a Softmax function is applied across the rows to form a probability distribution over the images, followed by categorical cross-entropy against the ground truth:
\[
\mathcal{L}_T = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} \log \frac{\exp(S_{j,j})}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \exp(S_{i,j})}
\]
The total loss is simply the average of the two directional losses:
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{CLIP}} = \frac{\mathcal{L}_I + \mathcal{L}_T}{2}
\]
Why use a symmetric cross-entropy loss? If the model optimized only row-wise (\(\mathcal{L}_I\)), it would learn to map images to text effectively, but the text encoder wouldn’t be explicitly penalized if multiple texts collapsed onto the same image region in representation space (and vice versa).
By enforcing symmetry:

The image encoder is forced to produce distinct, separable features for different images.
The text encoder is simultaneously forced to produce distinct, separable features for different captions.
Neither modality is allowed to dominate the shared embedding space.




Similarity matrix. Values on the main diagonal should be maximized, while the off-diagonal ones should be minimized


It is worth noting that the actual similarity score \(S_{i,j}\) is not just the cosine similarity (computed as the dot product of L2-normalized image and text embeddings, \(I_i\) and \(T_j\)), but it is also scaled by a learnable temperature parameter \(\tau\):
\[
S_{i,j} = \frac{I_i \cdot T_j}{\tau}
\]

title: CLIP — Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training
text:
Zero-Shot Classification
Classification is one of the foundational tasks in machine learning, particularly in computer vision. In standard supervised classification, given a data point and a set of predefined classes, the model outputs a probability distribution across those classes. However, those classes must be defined before training, restricting the model to categorizing data strictly within those labels.
A model capable of zero-shot classification, however, can categorize data into new classes without ever being explicitly trained on them. Because CLIP is trained to match images with descriptive text, we can construct a set of text prompts (e.g., “a photo of a dog” vs. “a photo of a cat”) and evaluate the similarity between an input image and each prompt. This turns classification into a dynamic search across arbitrary text labels. Even without dedicated training on a specific dataset or class list, CLIP can classify images flexibly on the fly.
In OpenAI’s original blog post, they show that CLIP can achieve performance similar to models that were trained for ImageNet, without using ImageNet for training at all. Furthermore, you can see in the figure below that CLIP keeps very high performance even when tested on other datasets, while the network trained for ImageNet shows degradation.



source:  OpenAI

title: CLIP — Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training
text:
More Uses
Beyond zero-shot classification, CLIP serves as a powerful foundational block for several downstream applications:
